speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO SELLING PRICE IN ALBERTA AND BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: I wish to direct a question to the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture. Will he say whether it is a fact that the dairy products board has permitted an increase in the selling price of butter in the province of Alberta, based on an increase in the price per pound of butterfat, but has refused to authorize a corresponding increase in British Columbia? If so, will the parliamentary assistant look into the reasons and give us an explanation at the first opportunity?

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert McCubbin (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO SELLING PRICE IN ALBERTA AND BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: This, Mr. Speaker, is something we have not heard of in our department. We are offering butter at 57 cents, basis Montreal. A spread of four cents is allowed to take care of handling, making into prints, and so on, bringing the figure to 61 cents. But neither I nor the department have heard that any ceiling has been placed upon the current make of butter. It is of course understood that the current production may be sold for whatever the trade likes. But the butter that is placed out by the government is 61 cents a pound, and I do not think you will find there is any difference between Alberta and British Columbia in this respect.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO SELLING PRICE IN ALBERTA AND BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: I should like to direct a supplementary question to the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture. The answer given by him was not very satisfactory, in view of the fact that I was in touch with British Columbia this morning and there is a variation of ten cents in the price of butterfat between Alberta and British Columbia. Will the parliamentary assistant investigate the matter and see that something is done?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO SELLING PRICE IN ALBERTA AND BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: Yes; that is being done now.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: OPPORTUNITY FOR PERSONNEL TO CONTRIBUTE TO FUND
speechtext: I should like to direct two questions to the Minister of National Defence, of which I have given notice. What steps are being taken to have all members of the permanent force elect to contribute to the pension fund under the Defence Services Pension Act, form 1 and form 1A? When a soldier does not have the information required, will this be supplied by the paymaster or other officials?

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxion (Minisier of National Defence):
subtopic: OPPORTUNITY FOR PERSONNEL TO CONTRIBUTE TO FUND
speechtext:
In answer to the first question, last year the three services called the attention of all units to a general order to give effect to the amendments adopted at the last session; and required commanding officers to give a certificate that every member of the unit under his command was, by December 1, 1950, advised of the additional opportunities presented as a result of the amendments to the Defence Services Pension Act. In addition, follow-ups have been sent by the chairman of the personnel members' committee to the officers commanding commands and formations both in Canada and outside, calling this to their attention.
With regard to the second question, the form, as the hon. member has pointed out to me privately, is necessarily complicated, and every man is given assistance in filling it out. It is quite unlikely that any man would have the information necessary to fill it out without access to the regimental and other records. The usual practice is for the form to be filled out by the paymaster or other appropriate officer working with the man, who then reads the form, makes his election, and signs the form.

maintopic: REPORTED USE OF COLOURING MATTER IN PRODUCTION OF BROWN LOAF
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this morning's press carries reports that the Canadians have suffered casualties in Korea. The reports go on to mention the names of certain officers leading in the current attacks. I would suggest that this is likely to cause considerable concern to the families of those officers. Will the Secretary of State for External Affairs make representations to United Nations officials requesting that the names of individual Canadians in action in Korea be deleted from press reports?

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: REPORTED USE OF COLOURING MATTER IN PRODUCTION OF BROWN LOAF
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would say that this would not be a matter for the United Nations as such, but possibly for the unified command, as the agency of the United Nations in Korea. I should be glad to discuss with my colleague the Minister of National Defence whether it would be appropriate or otherwise for the government to make representations on this matter.

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxton (Minister of National Defence):
maintopic: REPORTED USE OF COLOURING MATTER IN PRODUCTION OF BROWN LOAF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should supplement what was said by the Secretary of State for External Affairs about the reporting of casualties. We have asked the Canadian press not to report the names of Canadians suffering casualties. This is in accordance with the practice which we followed in both world wars, of endeavouring, by every means humanly possible, to get word to the next of kin first, before there was any mention of the names of those suffering casualties. In this our practice differs from that of some other countries, but we think our practice is right. We have asked that this be done, and it is being done.

Private Bills-Divorce
With regard to mention of individual officers in connection with actions, there is no doubt that that will cause anxiety to the next of kin of the officers mentioned. On the other hand, in the interests of keeping the Canadian people informed, it is desirable that as full a report be given of the actions engaged in as can properly be done without either giving comfort and assistance to the enemy or causing anxiety to the next of kin of the individuals concerned.
How this is to be done must be in part a matter of individual judgment and good practice, and I ask the co-operation of press correspondents in seeing that neither one thing nor the other is done-and this in addition to any rules of censorship, in respect of which we are working completely under the unified command. Because of this our press correspondents have to comply with precisely the same censorship provisions as other correspondents.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PLACE FARMERS IN PREFERRED CLASS AS TO PAYMENT FOR PRODUCTS DELIVERED FOR PROCESSING
AMENDMENT TO PLACE FARMERS IN PREFERRED CLASS AS TO PAYMENT FOR PRODUCTS DELIVERED FOR PROCESSING
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration the advisability of amending the Bank Act so as to place farmers in the same preferred class as labour, particularly in relation to protection for payments of farm produce delivered for processing.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the idea of this resolution came to my mind in consequence of failures of certain canning companies in Ontario with a resulting loss to hundreds of farmers. These failures cost the farmers of Ontario roughly $400,000 in 1949-50, money that they cannot afford to lose. Often companies go into bankruptcy after farmers have delivered their crops and before they are paid for them.
When the canning companies make their contracts, normally their credit situation has not reached a large amount, but in some cases later on the companies transfer to the banks complete coverage of the stock. The banks thereby assume ownership of the produce without the knowledge of the grower who has provided the raw material, without

. Bank Act
which the whole structure cannot function. Yet at the present time he is the one who provides the basis of finance.
In southern Ontario this section of the act has recently cost the growers who provide fruit and vegetables for processing several hundreds of thousands of dollars, partly because the bank, because of its preferred position, may not have kept close enough supervision of the activities of the company. Agriculture is not contesting the right of labour to be in a preferred position, but it feels that agricultural products should rank equally. The actual situation is that the most some creditors can normally lose is the pay due at the moment, while a farmer might lose the major portion of his year's income, or at least the whole of his fruit and vegetable crop. This could quite easily spell the loss of his farm if it is encumbered, as too many are.
In essence the situation is that without the raw products no canning company could operate. The grower turns his products over to the canning company without sufficient guarantee of payment and without sufficient knowledge of the stability of the company. The evil sometimes goes further than that; for growers are induced to invest in the companies in order to have a market for their goods.
The bank advances money, often for the express purpose of purchasing the raw products, but it exercises insufficient supervision to see that the money is used for the purpose for which the credit is extended. Often the money is used for other purposes, and when the crash comes the growers are the worst sufferers. The bank takes a lien on the finished products, mainly on the assumption that the growers have been paid. This resolution is not directed toward labour, but rather toward the whole of the preferred list.
We have no wish to place the canning companies or labour in any worse position than they are now, because they have their own troubles; but we would like the assurance that once a crop is sold to a company there will be some guarantee in case of failure, that the farmers will be allowed to come along with the preferred class of creditors. I should like this house to know that the farmer receives three cents or less for the green peas that go into a can, and he must pay $28 per acre for seed, fertilizer, trucking, and also his own wages and labour and all other expenses. From a ton of peas for which the farmer receives approximately $57, including seed, there will be produced well over 2,000 twenty-ounce cans, and now the new fifteen-ounce can is being used. In the case of tomatoes, com and asparagus, the rates are about the same.

I have received supporting letters to which I should like to refer. I received a letter from a marketing board in Ontario with 22,000 grower members; another with 3,000 growers; from an association of 300 growers, another of 150, and one large association made up of 12,500 members. There may be some overlapping in the membership of those organizations, because some farmers belong to more than one. I have also received a letter from a co-operative in Quebec.
To illustrate what may happen: A man in Norfolk county lost $6,500 on one crop of pears. When the affairs of the company are finally wound up he may receive ten per cent. I realize that this matter involves a process of law with which I am not familiar and which I am not competent to discuss. My purpose in moving this resolution was to bring the matter to the attention of the government and this house. I know that the questions I have raised are considered when the Bank Act comes up for periodical revision; therefore I ask permission to move that the debate on this resolution be adjourned until a later date.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.

speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the advisability of introducing legislation amending the Income Tax Act so as to permit taxpayers to deduct trade union dues, professional dues to teachers' organizations, and similar fees necessary to the earning of a livelihood, from their incomes before computing the amount of income tax to be paid.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the subject matter of this resolution has been before the house on a number of occasions. Mainly it has been brought to the attention of the house in the form of discussions and requests I have put to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) that the right set out in this motion be granted. On one occasion the subject matter of this resolution was before the house in the form of an amendment to the motion that Mr. Speaker do leave the chair for the house to go into committee of supply. That amendment was moved on October 31, 1949. It was debated on that day and then again on November 7, 1949. At the conclusion of the debate on the latter date a vote was taken and the amendment was defeated.
There are two differences between that amendment and the motion now before the house to which I should like to call attention. The first is as to the form of the motion, and

the other is as to the circumstances under which it is presented to the house. With regard to the form of the motion, I would point out that the amendment which was defeated on November 7, 1949, is found in Hansard at page 1292 and read as follows:
That all the words after the word "that" to the end of the question be struck out, and the following be substituted therefor:
"this house is of the opinion that the government should give consideration to the introduction of legislation amending the Income Tax Act so as to make it possible for taxpayers to deduct trade union dues from income before computing the amount of income tax to be paid."
The motion before the house today is almost the same as that, but there is an addition to which I should like to call attention. I shall explain later the reason for making that particular addition. The motion now before us reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the advisability of introducing legislation amending the Income Tax Act so as to permit taxpayers to deduct trade union-dues, professional dues to teachers' organizations, and similar fees necessary to the earning of a livelihood, from their incomes before computing the amount of income tax to be paid.
As must be obvious to those who have been following me, the difference in form is in the addition of the words, "professional dues to teachers' organizations, and similar fees necessary to the earning of a livelihood." A little later in my remarks I shall explain why I have felt it desirable and advisable to include, along with trade union dues in general, a specific reference to' the fees that teachers pay to their professional organizations.
The other difference to which I should like to call attention relates to the circumstances under which this matter is placed before the house. When I presented it to the house on October 31, 1949, it was, as I have already indicated, in the form of an amendment to a motion to go into committee of supply. A number of members indicated to me privately that they supported the substance of my amendment on that occasion, but that since it involved voting a want of confidence in the government they had no alternative but to vote against my amendment. Personally I think that defence has been worn threadbare, but government members still resort to it. As a matter of fact on that occasion one member on the government side stated quite clearly in his speech that he supported the amendment, only to vote against it when the vote was called.

I point out that the motion before the house today is a substantive motion that stands on its own feet. It is not an amendment to anything the government has proposed. It does not involve a vote of want of confidence. It is a motion asking the government to give consideration to the advisability of the course requested therein.
Incidentally I am pleased that the opportunity has come to present the motion to the house well in advance of the budget. We have not yet even been told the date on which the Minister of Finance will present the budget, so this is -a good time to make suggestions to the minister as to the taxation changes that he might propose in the budget.
I have no doubt that he is receiving many suggestions from organizations all across the country. Surely the high court of parliament should take advantage of that opportunity, and, if it agrees with the views set out in the motion, pass it and thereby suggest to the Minister of Finance that he should give consideration to this proposal.
I have taken a moment or two to emphasize the fact that this motion is not to be construed as a want of confidence motion as was the case on October 31 and November 7, 1949, and I hope that members on the government side who agree with the substance and the spirit of the motion will decide, this time, to vote for it.
In presenting this request that trade union dues, teachers' professional fees and similar dues necessary for the earning of a livelihood be allowed as income tax deductions before the income tax to be paid is computed, I recognize that the amount of money saved by the individual taxpayer is not very great. But it is a matter of principle, and I argue for it on two main counts. On the one hand I contend that it is only fair play, for reasons that I shall spell out in a moment; and on the other hand I remind hon. members that time and again it is said by representatives of all political parties that trade unions play a very important part in the life of our country. That is said particularly when elections are looming. Great appeals are made to the trade union movement, stressing the importance of the part that they play in the industrial and economic life of our country. That being the case, it seems to me that we ought to take every step that we can to make the members of the trade union movement feel that they really are a part of the picture in this country. I suggest that the recognition of their dues as deductible for income tax purposes would be a proper step in that direction.

Income Tax Deductions
To go back to my first point, namely, that I feel it should be done as a matter of fair play, I would point out that as the Income War Tax Act stood in the years 1945, 1946 and 1947, doctors, lawyers and teachers were given the right in those years to deduct their dues to their various societies for income tax purposes. I emphasize the point that that right was accorded to those groups of people in 1945, 1946 and 1947, whether they were on salaries or whether their income was from fees. As a matter of fact that distinction was settled in the Bond case, which went to the Exchequer Court of Canada. Mr. Bond, a lawyer, was an employee of the corporation of the city of Winnipeg, and he was on salary. It was contended by the income tax officials that therefore his case was different from that of lawyers making their living from the fees that they charged, and the income tax department had denied him the right to deduct his fees to the law society for income tax purposes.
The exchequer court decided in Mr. Bond's favour and made it clear that as the law stood in the years 1945, 1946 and 1947 the groups of persons to whom I have referred were entitled to deduct their professional fees for income tax purposes, whether they were on salaries or on gross incomes from fees. It transpired later that trade unionists were similarly entitled, under the law as it stood in 1945, 1946 and 1947, to deduct their trade union dues for income tax purposes. I say it transpired later that they had that right under the law, but in point of fact they were denied that right by a ruling of the income tax department, even though the law gave it to them in 1945, 1946 and 1947.
The income tax department ruled that these people were in a different category, that their wages were to be treated as net, and that what they paid for trade union dues could not be deducted. As a result of that discriminatory decision on the part of the income tax department another case was taken to the Exchequer Court of Canada. I am referring now to the Cooper case, Mr. Cooper being a moving picture projectionist. Like the lawyer, Mr. Bond, to whom I referred a few moments ago, Mr. Cooper was also from the city of Winnipeg. The exchequer court made its decision with respect to the Cooper case in June, 1949, but the case was taken there in April, 1948. Let me jump ahead to the decision.
The decision of Mr. Justice Angers of the Exchequer Court of Canada was that as the law stood in 1945, 1946 and 1947, Mr. Cooper and his fellow moving picture projectionists should have been entitled to deduct their
trade union dues for income tax purposes, and the implication was that the same right extended to other trade unionists. Let me be perfectly fair, and say that there might have been some doubt as to whether it extended to all trade union dues, but certainly it was clear that it did extend to trade union dues in the case of those in closed shops, in union shops or in shops covered by the Rand formula.
The income tax department accepted the decision and announced in the fall of 1949 that any cases not statute-barred would be reviewed. That meant very little. It meant only that trade unionists who had actually applied for this reduction when they filed their returns for 1945, 1946 and 1947, if they met certain other conditions, might apply for a refund. As a matter of fact most trade unionists had not claimed their deduction for those taxation years because, despite what the law said, despite the fact that doctors, lawyers and teachers were making their deductions, the income tax department had ruled that this right did not extend to trade unionists. So it can be said for the income tax department that in the fall of 1949 they carried out the letter of the decision of Mr. Justice Angers, but it had very little effect.
What had happened in the meantime? As I say, the law was clear for 1945, 1946 and 1947, and it is clear now that the law should have extended to trade unionists the right that was extended in those years to doctors, lawyers and teachers. Mr. Cooper took his case to the exchequer court in April, 1948. By a strange coincidence, in May, 1948, only a month later, the government introduced amendments to the then Income War Tax Act. In 1948 we did two jobs in the field of income tax legislation; we amended the old Income War Tax Act for 1948, and we also passed a new Income Tax Act which was to come into effect on January 1, 1949.
We now find that, once it became law, the resolution introduced by the government in May, 1948, had the effect of denying for 1948 the right of trade unionists to claim trade union dues as a deduction, and it also had the effect of taking away that right from teachers, who had enjoyed it in 1945, 1946 and 1947. That explains why I have made special reference to teachers in this resolution. I believe they have a special word coming to them because of the way that right, which they enjoyed in the years I mentioned, was taken away from them so far as 1948 and subsequent years were concerned.
The same change made in 1948 drew a line right down the middle of two groups of people, doctors and lawyers. Previously all


doctors and lawyers had the right to deduct the fees they paid their associations. After the adoption of the amendment which was put through the house in 1948 those doctors and lawyers working for fees, working for individual patients and clients and collecting fees, paying expenses, office rent, help, and so on, still had the right to include among their deductions the fees they paid the medical or law society; but a doctor or lawyer who worked solely for a company and was on salary was not permitted to deduct his fees to the medical or law society. Frankly, my main concern in bringing this matter before the house is the case of the trade unionists and school teachers, but in all fairness I must say that I do not like the discrimination now made between these two groups of doctors and lawyers. If in both cases they have to pay these fees in order to carry on their practice, it seems to me that in both cases they should be allowed those fees as a deduction.
That change, as I say, was made by amending the Income War Tax Act in 1948. Someone may ask the question, "Were you not here then? Why did you not stand in the way of it at that time?" That is a very fair question. I have read before, and I read again today, the debate relating to that change. I find that it took place on June 2, 1948, and covers several pages of Hansard, commencing at page 4683. The budget resolution before us dealt with the deduction allowances to be made to railway employees in certain Categories, and travelling salesmen. I find that the main point being emphasized then was that a discrimination which had previously existed as between train conductors and engine crews on the one hand, and sleeping car conductors and porters on the other, was being wiped out by statute. For a period of time previously train conductors and engine crews were permitted to deduct their away-from-home expenses when they had to lie over at the other end of the journey, but that right was denied to the sleeping car conductors and porters, who might be on the same train. Well, we fought that out here a good many times, and when this amendment I am talking about was before the house in the form of a budget resolution on June 2, 1948, the minister emphasized that this discrimination had already been done away with by a ruling in the department, and that the effect of this amendment was to confirm that change.
Well, it was all to the good; we all accepted it. The whole tone of the minister's remarks and of the entire debate was that this change was in the nature of a concession. An
Income Tax Deductions allowance that had previously been given to only a few people was now extended to others, so the house accepted it as a concession to requests which had been made in this chamber and approved it readily. In fact the house approved the principle involved in that change so readily that when on June 23, 1948, we had before us the bill with the precise words of section 3 in it, it was not discussed at all. At page 5699 of Hansard for that date there is the notation, "Sections 1 to 5 inclusive agreed to." No one said a word. Everyone was satisfied that section 3, which was included in the group carried so readily, was something we all wanted. There was nothing in the discussion or in what the Minister of Finance said during that debate to indicate that in this resolution there was anything restrictive in character. After it got on the statute book, however-indeed, the next year, 1949- we began to discover that section 3 of chapter 53 of the statutes of 1948, which wrote a new section 6 into the basic Income War Tax Act, not only gave something but also took something away. It gave sleeping car conductors and porters the right to deduct away-from-home expenses; that was good; but it also had tucked into it wording which meant that all salaries and wages were henceforth to be regarded as net. The result of that wording is that it has now been ruled that trade union dues, teachers' fees, and doctors' and lawyers' fees in cases where the taxpayer is on salary, cannot be deducted.
I know quite well that what is said on the floor of parliament does not carry the weight that we sometimes think it should carry when courts deal with these matters. I again discovered that to be so a few days ago in reading the report of Mr. Justice Kellock with regard to the railway dispute of last fall. He makes it clear that although certain things were in the preamble to the bill, and although certain things were said on the floor of parliament, what he had to be governed by was the wording of the statute itself. I therefore realize that we cannot ask the courts to be governed by what was said on the floor of parliament when this section 3 of chapter 53 of the statutes of 1948 was discussed on June 2, 1948. But in all fairness I submit that this house should rectify what was done on that occasion. This house had no notion-I am satisfied that nobody in the house was aware of it, unless it was the Minister of Finance-that on that occasion a section was being written into the Income War Tax Act which was going to take something away. We knew it was going to give something, and we approved what it was giving. But we learned a year later that it was taking away a right which teachers had

Income Tax Deductions enjoyed and which some doctors and some lawyers had enjoyed. We also learned that it took away for the year 1948 a right which in 1949 Mr. Justice Angers said trade unionists should have had for the years 1945, 1946 and 1947.
I have just made the statement that it was the next year before we knew about this matter. Here on my desk I have a great many papers, too many to bother picking them all up; but amongst them is a copy of the Saskatchewan Teachers' Bulletin, put out early in the year 1949, in which the Saskatchewan teachers' federation reminded their members that the fees to their federation were deductible for income tax purposes. They still thought, in 1949, that the law was as it had been; and it was not until the fall of that year that they were notified that in their spring bulletin they had said something which was not correct. Others were in a similar situation. It was not until 1949, when people were filing their income tax returns, that news really got around as to the change that had been made by that section 3 of chapter 53 of the statutes of 1948.
I would point out that that chapter 53 of the statutes of 1948 was to all intents and purposes just a one-year statute. It amended the old Income War Tax Act, which had been on the statute book ever since world war I, making certain changes that applied for the year 1948. In the same session we passed chapter 52 of the statutes of 1948, which was the new Income Tax Aet which was1 to go into effect on January 1, 1949; and that is the income tax legislation under which we are now functioning. That chapter 52 carried forward for the year 1949 and subsequent years the same limiting provision that was enacted by section 3 of chapter 53. We now have the situation that apparently what the government wanted has been made law, despite the decision of the Exchequer Court of Canada to the effect that trade unionists had been denied, by ruling of the income tax department, something that was their right back in 1945, 1946 and 1947.
It seems clear to me that the way to wipe out this injustice of the past, this discriminatory story that we have had with respect to this matter, is for parliament to -ask the government to reconsider the whole position. That is what my motion does.
I repeat to all hon. members opposite, since it is a matter of concern to them, that my motion is not a want of confidence motion; it is a request that the government give consideration to this matter. What we request is simply that they consider the advisability of allowing as deductions for income tax purposes trade union dues and

fees to professional societies, such as teachers' societies and others, where those dues or fees are necessary to the earning of a livelihood. No one denies that in most if not all cases these dues are necessary to the earning of a livelihood. I am told by my lawyer friends that they cannot practice unless they pay their fees to the law society. I am told by my medical friends that they have to pay their fees to the medical society. I know that, in many if not all of the provinces, teachers certainly have to pay their fees to their teachers' professional societies in order to be able to teach. As to trade unionists, there are many closed shops and union shops in which a man cannot hold his job unless he carries his union card and is paid up and in good standing. There are other shops which are covered by the Rand formula and in which it is necessary not only for the members of the trade unions to pay their dues but for all others working in that plant to do so, even though they are not members of any union. In addition to the plants where trade union membership is a condition of employment, the fact of the matter is that the conditions of employment that are obtained by many workers are the direct result of the money they pay in trade union dues. I therefore submit that since the fees that are paid by these various groups of people are all necessary to the gaining of a livelihood, they should be allowed as deductions for income tax purposes.
I hope there will not be any objection to this motion on the ground that it would be difficult to determine which are bona fide dues and so on. That point is easy to deal with, I do not mind if the government insists that, in the case of trade unions, it apply only where a union has been certified, if you will, under a federal code or under a provincial code. Personally I should like to see it given to all unions, even to those that are seeking certification. But at any rate some provision could be worked out to satisfy the government as to the bona fides of any claims made under this provision; and I am sure that similarly there will be no difficulty in establishing the right of teachers, doctors, lawyers and any others who have to pay fees in this way in order to earn their livelihood.
I want to say frankly and categorically, Mr. Speaker, that legislation giving effect to this principle would be a slight encouragement to trade unions. The amount of money saved by the individual member of the trade union is only a few cents in some cases, and a few dollars in others. In the Cooper case, which went to the exchequer court, I think the saving involved was only about $35. Of course Mr. Cooper got back his expenses,

which were considerable. The principle is one which means a great deal to trade unionists and to people in similar situations. As I said, it would encourage trade unionists to a slight extent. I hope that will not be the reason why this resolution is turned down. I hope that hon. members will think seriously about it before they cast a vote against it. The last time it was before the house, 48 members voted for it. If it comes to a vote today-in other words if the government is not prepared to accept it and make it unanimous-I certainly hope that the number who vote for it will be increased considerably.
I have presented the story of this matter over these past few years, and I repeat the two points that I made earlier in my remarks.
I think this motion should be passed on two grounds.
On the one hand, I think it should be passed on the grounds of fair play as between various groups in our community. I think it should be passed as a matter of fair play, as a matter of rectifying the injustice, the discrimination trade unionists suffered at the hands of the income tax department's decision back in 1945, 1946 and 1947, during the years when, according to Mr. Justice Angers, the law gave them this right.
My other main argument is that since we all recognize that trade unionists play an important part in the life of our country, surely we should take steps of this kind, which are designed to help trade unionists feel that they are recognized as part of the industrial and economic life of this country. I am very glad to add the suggestion that teachers should be treated likewise. I am prepared to argue that so far as doctors and lawyers are concerned, and any others, they should ibe in the same category. The point is, let us be completely fair in our income tax legislation. On that basis I urge the adoption of this resolution,

The question of union dues being deducted from total income for income tax purposes has been discussed before. I feel that although trade unionism is not a profession in the sense that doctors and lawyers are members of a profession, or school teachers and nurses are members of a profession, yet trade unionists have a very important part to play in the economy of Canada.
When we have on the statute books legislation which provides* that certain groups may deduct their dues or fees, and at the same time prevents others from doing the same, it does leave a measure of what may be termed -and I think the only measure of-class legislation. It is on that basis that I should like to see this discriminatory legislation removed. Everyone should receive the same treatment.
The trade unionists who do not work in a closed shop or a union shop are probably in this position. In some cases they constitute 65 per cent or 75 per cent of the employees, but they are carrying the full cost of the administration of the union. They have to negotiate with management and they incur considerable expenses. There are officials who are on full time in the unions, and they have to be paid. In this way, 65 per cent to 75 per cent of the employable employees are paying the costs of the benefits which 100 per cent of the employees receive. If the dues were deductible for income tax

Income Tax Deductions purposes it would be a measure of recognition to those people who are carrying the burden, and it would be somewhat less costly to them. At the present time they have their union dues plus the cost of their income tax. The union dues must carry on. If these extra charges could be removed it would be a help.
As has been outlined by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, this is not a want of confidence motion in the government, and I am prepared to support it.

I am against the legislation because it represents gross discrimination; it is what someone has called class legislation. I do not like that expression when used in Canada because I do not think we admit the existence of classes, as they exist in certain other countries.
Let me endorse what has been said by the mover of the resolution. He mentioned school teachers and, of course, I am interested in that phase of the matter. As an active teacher in Saskatchewan my experience was that these fees were simply deducted from my salary cheque. A teacher in Saskatchewan has no option when it comes to the payment of professional fees: if he does not pay them, he does not teach; if he teaches, they are deducted from his pay, and there the matter rests.
I have a good deal of objection to the way in which the government changed the regulation. In 1945, 1946 and 1947 these fees

Income Tax Deductions were exempt tor income tax purposes. The manner of the change was astonishing. The new regulation was defined as becoming applicable on January 1, 1948. The teachers in Saskatchewan as such were not notified about the change in the regulations. I suppose they were supposed to know what had happened. In fact the Teachers' Bulletin, for February, 1949, addressing itself to its members has this to say:
If your income tax return is filed late there is a penalty. You are reminded that federation fees are an allowable deduction.
It was only after some months that the teachers discovered, that is those who had filed their income tax returns, that they had to go into the whole matter again and that that right was being taken away. I appeal for the passage of this resolution on the grounds of equity and fair play. I have no objection whatever to the allowance of professional fees, either medical or legal. I think they should be exempt, but if they are exempt, I cannot understand why teachers' fees are not.
I want to go a step further. In moving this resolution I think my hon. friend had in mind particularly the exemption of trade union dues. I am in support of that. Speaking in this house on November 7, 1949, the last time this matter was brought up, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) said, as reported on page 1494 of Hansard of November 7, 1949:
We have considered the matter, and perhaps it should be adopted.
The "it" being the amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). The minister went on to say:
Perhaps it is something to which we will come. It is certainly administratively practical.
I think the time has now come. There should be no discrimination and the government should act fairly in dealing with persons in all professions and trades who must belong to an association in order to earn their living.

speakeroldname: Mr. James Sinclair (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) is presently receiving some delegations on tax matters and I have been asked to say a few words. I did not come prepared because this matter has been dealt with each year by the Minister of Finance when similar resolutions or amendments have been introduced. In his speech the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) touched fairly on the actual facts of the case with respect to the judgments which were given in connection

with the Income War Tax Act. However, he did not touch in any way on what is the main problem in this resolution.
The fundamental problem in all tax systems is as to where you draw the line between what is taxable and non-taxable. In the short experience which I have had in this house with tax measures and putting through budget resolutions each spring I have always found that point to be the most difficult. For example, in the excise tax law there is always the question as to whether goods are properly semi-luxuries or necessities. Each hon. member of this house can think of some goods for which a special plea can be made that they be placed in the lighter tax group.
So too in the matter of income tax. Let us be fair about this and admit that no one likes taxes. Taxes are especially unpopular with members of parliament because they are held responsible by their constituents for the imposition of those taxes. I have been doing quite a bit of reading recently on income tax. I find that today we seem to be much more tolerant toward taxes, especially income taxes, than they were when the tax was first evolved. Pitt was the first to introduce income tax in the modern British parliament in order to help finance the Napoleonic wars. So distasteful was the tax that at the time the period of the tax ended Lord Brougham ordered all records and documents to be burned so that no future government would have any income tax information which had been assembled at the time.
The responsibility on the minister, whether he be the Chancellor of the Exchequer in Great Britain or the Minister of Finance here, is to make any tax system as fair as possible, to make it understandable, to make whatever borderline he draws easily understood and easily enforceable. I think that is one of the most difficult problems in connection with taxation.
Coming now to the actual question under review, the matter of income tax exemptions, it has been a basic concept in both British and Canadian income tax laws to regard salaries and wages as net income, and so subject to income tax. On the other hand, those who are self-employed, those who have to spend money to make money, have always been regarded as having the right to make as deductions those expenses which are necessary to earn the income which they have earned. So we have the immediate difference established between those who are employed and those who are self-employed.
The person who is employed naturally tries to see that his salary or wage is set at a level which will cover all the factors he

must meet in earning his living and meeting the cost of living, including for example his professional fees. The man who is selfemployed must naturally try to make his business or his occupation or his profession so successful that he will be able to pay the expenses which are necessary to earn his income.
That leads us along to this one major difference, as far as the subject matter of this resolution is concerned, between those who are self-employed and those who are not. The doctor, lawyer, teacher or professional man, or the non-professional man or tradesman, who works for a salary or wages, has that salary or wages regarded by the income tax law of this country as being taxable income from which the statutory exemptions granted by parliament for dependents, married status, extra medical expenses and so forth may be deductible. But that is his taxable income.
On the other hand, the doctor, lawyer, teacher, or tradesman who is in business for himself is allowed to make as deductions from his gross earnings those outlays which are necessary to earn that income. That brings us to this matter of the closed shop. If a union man, say a plumber who is working for himself, should find it necessary that he belong to a union because of a closed shop agreement, his dues would be a deductible allowance. If a businessman or a doctor or a lawyer who is not being paid a fixed amount by a hospital or some other organization finds that he must belong to a professional organization in order to work- and these professional organizations are the closest thing to a union closed shop you can find except that the professions do not like the phrase applied to them-the fee he must pay is regarded as a proper business expense because he could not be in business unless he belonged to that organization.
For that reason there has been a distinction between those receiving salaries or wages and those who are self-employed. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre made much of the court interpretations of the provisions of the Income War Tax Act, 1945-46 and 1947, and that a judicial ruling had been given that these dues were deductible in the case of those who were not self-employed. He stated also that it was unfair that the Department of Finance took immediate action once those rulings were handed down to get back to what has been the intent in the income tax law in Canada since we have had an income tax, that is, to regard salaries and wages as net taxable income.

There are a lot of clever lawyers throughout the country-there are a lot of clever lawyers in this House of Commons-who are always busy at the law, and especially the income tax law of this country, trying to find loopholes. If the department did not take corrective action when such a loophole has been found then our whole tax structure would pretty soon dissipate. Clever lawyers can always find some point to take to the courts, and now and again they get nterpre-tations which were not the intent of the law as framed. I can give examples, and hon. members can remember examples. In the eleven years that I have been in the house corrections have been made, but I have never seen a tax measure made retroactive to cover such loopholes, but the hon. member may be able to correct me.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: This particular law, chapter 53 of the statutes of 1948, which was passed in June of that year, was made retroactive to January 1, 1948.
That is the practice in every budget.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: As pointed out by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), it is the practice with every budget that the actual budget proposals should apply from the beginning of the fiscal year-as far as income taxes are concerned, but not so far as excise taxes are concerned, which generally have a midnight dateline on the budget day.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Not always with regard to income tax either.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Coming to the point of fair play mentioned by the member, because the courts ruled that the phrasing of the law at that time permitted a deduction of dues, the hon. member suggests that it is only fair to continue that. If that were the case there are many corporation lawyers in Canada who would like to have that outlook sustained, men who have found ways to get around the provisions in the tax laws made by parliament. The proper course to follow is that which the department has always followed. When judicial rulings based on the act have been made which have not been what was meant at the time the act was passed, the department has taken corrective action.
The hon. member went on to point out that certainly in the case of closed shops, or where the Rand formula applied, union dues had to be paid and were a cost of the occupation of the men concerned. That is quite true; but once again, if we enter that field, where are we going to stop? Certainly the cost to the man of going to his work in the morning and of coming home at night is also a cost of his

Income Tax Deductions occupation. There are professional courses he must take to improve himself and professional tools that he must buy. All these things to the man on salary or wages are a cost of working. We could start today with the proposal of the mover of the motion and step by step broaden our income tax law to include more and more of these very desirable exemptions which members are always so keen to put forward in order to secure exemptions for other groups. The hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. Higgins), for example, just a moment ago mentioned a special group, radiologists.
These things would lead to a constantly diminishing rate of net taxable income but would not in any way relieve the country from having to raise the revenues we must have for the management of the country. Therefore you might have a lower net taxable income but you are going to have higher rates thereon. These are the points that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has made to the house in previous years, the fact that so far as a workable tax law is concerned the British and Canadians have always regarded salaries and wages as net taxable income. Men who accept positions on salaries or wages must always have in their minds the obligations they must meet out of those salaries and wages and try to secure adequate pay.
The second thing is that this line on taxable income is a very easy line understood by the people. It is a line very easily enforced so far as the department is concerned with a minimum of administration and evasion. These views have been put forward by the minister on earlier occasions. The government has, as the resolution asks, given consideration to allowing such fees or dues to be deducted from the wages or salaries of people paid in that way, and the Minister of Finance has told me to say that the government cannot accept the proposal for the reasons I have repeated.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the resolution was introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), although I was not here when he spoke to it I assume he did not leave very much for anyone else to say that would be at all new. All I want to do is to give my support to the proposals in the resolution, and in doing so to reply to one statement made by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair), who has just taken his seat. He asked where the matter was going to end if exemption of union dues for income tax purposes was allowed. He wanted to know where we would draw the line. As a Liberal, surely he will

agree that the place to draw the line is where the same principles will apply to everybody.
To the extent that any tax does not apply to everybody in the same way then it is discriminatory, and in this case it is discriminatory against trade unionists and in favour of professional men and women. Today it is becoming more and more the general practice that the ordinary worker must be a member of a trade union if he is going to work at his particular trade, in the same way that a lawyer must be a member of the legal associations of his profession if he is going to practise law. As a matter of fact I think lawyers go a great deal further than trade unionists. My attention was drawn to the fact that recently a notable lawyer, whose home is in one province, had to go to the province of British Columbia to defend a case, and he had to pay the initiation fee of the law society of that province although he was already a member of the law society of his own province. The initiation fee, or whatever it is called in the profession, is quite sizeable. I think in this case it was $1,500, and I would imagine that he would be able to deduct that.
That is a capital expenditure.

If not then he would be able to deduct the fee he paid to the law society of his own province. All that the motion asks, and all that we have been asking in this house for the past few years, is that the same law apply to trade unionists as to members of the professions. I regret very much that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has decided that he must continue to discriminate against trade unionists because, I assume, trade unionists are small fry with whom he need not be concerned.

Mr. Speaker, I have been listening to the debate on the resolution for a long time. Something was said about class legislation. While we have been dealing entirely with labour we must also remember that the farmers of Canada have associations to which they pay dues, and that they are not entitled to deduct their dues or contributions for income tax purposes. Until such time as the entire question can be considered I do not think I would be willing to support the resolution. The amount involved is very small, possibly something under $3 per individual, so it would not make

very much difference to anyone as far as the cost of living is concerned.

It is a matter of principle.
You do not advocate discrimination, do you?

Mr. Speaker, I derived a great deal of pleasure from listening to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) this afternoon, and the other speakers who have taken part in this debate. I was hoping all the reasons that could be advanced both for and against this resolution would be brought forward so there would be no occasion for me to speak, but the reason I cannot support it has not been put forward, so I am going to take this opportunity to mention it. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre stated that the last time this subject was discussed the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) had given reasons for supporting the resolution, but then voted against it. I believe his vote was communicated to his constituency just as mine was, and I have no doubt be explained it just as I did. I pointed out that it had been brought forward as a want of confidence motion in the government instead of being dealt with on its merits, which took care of that particular vote; but I went on to say that there were arguments both for and against the resolution, and my vote on that occasion did not indicate how I might vote if it was dealt with on its merits.
This afternoon there will be a vote, and I am sure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would say that today the resolution is going to be dealt with on its merits-that is, unless all the Liberals happen to vote one way and all the opposition vote the other way. In that case perhaps he or someone else will suggest that this was done because some sinister individual behind the curtains somewhere said they should vote that way. That is not why I will be voting against this resolution, however. Mention has been made of class legislation and discrimination, suggesting that anyone voting against this resolution would be voting in favour of both class legislation and discrimination. I find that the community is divided into many groups. There is the industrial group represented by the unions; and rightly so, because the little man in industry, with no one to speak for him, is liable to suffer unless he organizes with others to take care of injustices like these. That is bound to be the case with the world as it is and human beings as they are. The same thing applies in agriculture; the farmer alone is liable to be pinched, so he gets together with other farmers in agricultural organizations. It is the same with businessmen; they get together in their groups.
Income Tax Deductions Because the world is such a complex place, eventually more and more groups will be organized, not against other groups but to see that their members have a fair hearing and are dealt with justly. Our job here is to see that as between groups everyone gets a fair hearing and is fairly dealt with.
Among my constituents there are a great many trade union members, and a great many farmers, who are also organized. However, there are also many fishermen, who are not organized, many trappers, who are not organized, and other unorganized groups. To vote for this resolution at this time, I think, would be taking a step that would make it more difficult for the Minister of Finance to collect the money necessary to make the tremendous expenditures that will have to be made, and to support this resolution would not be dealing fairly with all those others who are not able to have someone speak for them in this house. The unions have members to speak forcibly for them, and the farm organizations have members to speak for them. As the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) was going out I jokingly said to him, "I thought you would stay here and speak for the farmers, and perhaps suggest that the final payment under the five-year wheat agreement might be exempt from income tax." He replied that he was not going to make that suggestion, but if anyone else did he would be glad to support it.
The hon. member said a line had been drawn dividing the doctors and lawyers. He did not mention anything about engineers. I pay dues to an engineering society, and I have never dreamed of claiming those as a deduction. Businessmen pay dues to chambers of commerce and other organizations, and so on. Then I think of all those who could not come under such legislation; and because the doctors and lawyers have that privilege it seems to me the resolution is saying that since we cannot get the doctors and lawyers off that basis we should take the mountain to Mahomet and see that as many others as possible get on the same basis. If some time in the future, in order to do away with a discrimination which the hon. member believes exists, he would bring in a resolution that would tend to simplify the income tax return, eliminate the small proportion of doctors and lawyers who now deduct their fees, and at the same time enable the people in whom he is interested to regain their position, that might be worthy of consideration. However, I am afraid I cannot support any proposal which would make our income tax forms much more complicated at this time in our history.

I wish to avail myself of the opportunity to close the debate, because I believe the remarks of the hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. Major), the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Weaver) and the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sinclair) do deserve consideration. I want to thank the parliamentary assistant for his reference to the fair and accurate manner in which I presented the facts relating to this whole question. I appreciate, too, that he made his arguments quite clear, because it seems to me the two main arguments he presented are very easy to meet, and I shall endeavour to meet them. However, I will save the parliamentary assistant until later and deal with the other two hon. members first. After all, parliamentary assistants should have some standing around this place, in view of all the cracks that are made about them.
May I say to the hon. member for Glengarry, as well as to the hon. member for Churchill with respect to part of what he said, that the resolution is worded to include farmers, engineers and others, the very groups for whom they speak. I ask hon. members to note that I did not stop at trade union dues, but went on to say "professional dues to teachers' organizations, and similar fees necessary to the earning of a livelihood." Those words are quoted directly from the resolution. I point out that I and others have had a good deal to say about doctors and lawyers, but doctors and lawyers are not mentioned in the resolution. I mentioned trade union dues particularly, because I feel trade unionists got a particularly raw deal in that they were denied the right to deduct those dues for income tax purposes during the years the law allowed it. I mentioned teachers particularly because I felt that they got a raw deal in that, having had the privilege of making those deductions, that privilege was taken away from them in the manner which was described both by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) and myself.
What about accountants?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

The hon. member for St.
Paul's (Mr. Rooney) asks:	what about
accountants? All these other people are included in that general phrase "and similar fees necessary to the earning of a livelihood." As a matter of fact, a good many of those people-farmers, engineers in some cases, and accountants in some cases also-are in
[Mr Knowles.]
the category of persons whose income is on a gross basis. Those who are on a gross basis, as is the case with doctors and lawyers at the present time, have the right now to deduct expenses necessary to the earning of their gross income. To farmers, to engineers and to accountants who are on a gross basis I suggest that they do not need legislation but that the act now permits, in the case of those whose income is gross, deduction of the amounts they expend in the earning of that income. I am right with them.
There is, Mr. Speaker, an attempt to misinterpret or misunderstand this motion, if there is any suggestion that its purpose is to bring in class legislation. The purpose, Mr. Speaker, is the very opposite. The very wording of the resolution makes clear that its purpose is to end class legislation and to extend to all persons the right to deduct for income tax purposes the amounts necessarily expended in the earning of a livelihood, where those amounts are in the nature of fees to unions or societies or associations of one kind or another. I hope that is perfectly clear. I remember that once before, when this matter was up for discussion, the Ottawa Journal made the same comment. I am surprised to hear the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Weaver) and the hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. Major) express the views that were expressed on the editorial page of the Ottawa Journal. They thought that what was wrong with this suggestion was that it was class legislation. Not at all, Mr. Speaker. It is class legislation the way it now is. My request to the government-

The difference between the wording of the two meets the very point that

the hon. member for Churchill and the hon. member for Glengarry have raised. There is no argument on the point. I am with them one hundred per cent that this right I am asking for people to whom it has been denied should be extended to all who have to pay out any kind of fee necessarily for the purpose of earning a livelihood.
Before I leave the hon. member for Churchill, I must say that he disappointed me a little bit this afternoon. He started out by saying that part of the reason for his vote on November 7, 1949, when he voted against my amendment on that occasion, had been stated by me and by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) when we referred to the position that government members find themselves in when there is before the house an amendment that is in effect a vote of want of confidence. I am glad that the hon.
member was not trying to set a trap for

It is not in order to refer to other motions that have been discussed in this session, but I can think of other debates in which members on the government side have said that if my colleague had only worded the motion in such a way, it would have been better. But if my colleague had done so, the request from the government side would have been to word it the other way.
I am still anxious to get around to my friend the hon. member for Coast-Capilano, and he is sitting over there on tenterhooks too. The hon. member for Coast-Capilano discussed the question discursively in part but in the main he got down to two general arguments. One of his arguments was that the government was perfectly right and that it was to be defended for its action in 1948 in changing the law to carry out what had been its intention in the years 1945, 1946 and 1947. There is no question as to what the intention of the government was in those previous years, because the ruling of the Department of National Revenue carried out that intention.
The hon. member says that the government is to be commended for changing the law so as to carry out what had been its intention. Well, Mr. Speaker, this is like the discussion the hon. member for Vancouver South and I have been having. The question of intention comes up time and again. I must refer to the most recent example, the one that is in my mind at the moment, namely, the Kellock report in reference to the railway dispute of last fall. It was said on the floor of this house that it was the intention of the government that the workers involved in that dispute should not be asked to accept legislation that was discriminatory as between one group and another. That same intention was expressed in the preamble to Bill No. 1, which was before parliament last fall. We were asked on the floor of parliament to accept the government's word that that meant that the hotel and water transport workers would get the same deal as the railway employees got. And I can say that the union leaders, too, thought that that was the case; but when Mr. Justice Kellock made his report he said in it-I was quoting from it in another connection the other night, and I could give the quotation, but I know it very well, in spirit at any rate. He said that the employees drew two things to his attention: one, the wording of the preamble, and two, statements of intention made on the floor of parliament. But he made it clear

that he had to be governed not by the preamble, not by the intention of the government or the intention of parliament but by what was in the statute.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

It is something like the reference made the other night by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. Higgins). The hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) says that a line has to be drawn. Then he says that the place to draw that line is with respect to net income. That is, to draw it as between net income and gross income. The decision of the government has been that in the case of net income there are to be no deductions, no deductions except those provided for in the act. What a way to draw a line! You draw a firm line, and no deductions are to be allowed; but in the very act in which you draw that line you proceed to make certain exceptions. Well, all we are asking is that there be included in those exceptions to that line which has been drawn exceptions which are necessary to achieve fair play.
There are certain cases where, despite the line that has been drawn which says that net income must be fully taxable, exceptions are allowed. For example, a single clergyman maintaining a dwelling is allowed certain deductions from his net income as a clergyman. Clergymen operating cars, even though on a net income, are allowed certain deductions. Transport workers on salary in certain cases, those men who have to lie overnight away from home, are allowed deductions from net wages for those away-from-home expenses. The same is true of travelling salesmen under certain conditions that are spelled out in the act and regulations. These are all cases of men on net salaries. They are allowed those deductions.
Family allowances are an addition to our income, on which there is no taxation. I hope I do not draw the abuse of other hon. members if I refer to the fact that part of our income, and the income of members in certain legislatures in this country, is not taxable because we have to spend that part, all of it, and more in some cases, in connection with the earning of the rest of our income. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it is illusory to say that the government's decision is based on this unctuous principle that we have drawn a line. The line has been crossed so many times that

Income Tax Deductions it is shattered and there is nothing unreasonable about the request that one of the exceptions to that line be this business of trade union dues, teachers' professional dues to their societies and the fees of any others, farmers, engineers, accountants, and all the rest who have to pay these fees in order to carry on their particular occupation.
I remind the government that we used to get the same argument about drawing a line from Mr. Ilsley when he was minister of finance in relation to one particular group of people. I refer to sleeping car conductors and sleeping car porters. I referred to them earlier today, but the position taken by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano makes me refer to them again. I used to complain year in and year out, as I still complain year in and year out about some other things, about the fact that train conductors, engine crews and so on, when they were away from home were allowed to deduct from their wages their away-from-home expenses before computing their income tax, but that sleeping car conductors and sleeping car porters, riding on the same train, in some instances lying overnight in the same place, were not allowed to make these deductions.
The former minister of finance (Mr. Ilsley) used to express great sympathy with my protest against this discrimination made on the floor. Both of us wanted the train conductors and engine crews to have that deduction, but I wanted the others to have it too. "But", said Mr. Ilsley, "you have to draw a line." That is exactly the same line my hon. friend is giving us today. The line then was a little different. The line at that time was between a monthly salary and an hourly wage.
How ridiculous!-that because sleeping car conductors and sleeping car porters were on monthly salaries, and train conductors and engineers were on hourly wages, one was allowed to deduct his away-from-home expenses and the other was not. But, year after year, for a great many years, Mr. Ilsley stood up and said, "I appreciate the point made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), but you have to draw a line somewhere".
Well, the day came when, because of representations on that point, the government realized that that line had to be abolished. The irony of the story is that it was the very section which abolished that line of discrimination against sleeping car conductors and sleeping car porters which created this new line of discrimination against trade unionists. It was that very section, section 3 of chapter 53 of the statutes of 1948, which wiped out the old line but,
