subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE AS TO APPLICATION OF PRINCIPLE BY DEMOCRACIES WITHIN UNITED NATIONS
PROPOSED CONFERENCE AS TO APPLICATION OF PRINCIPLE BY DEMOCRACIES WITHIN UNITED NATIONS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration the advisability of supporting the calling of a convention of delegates from the democracies which sponsored the North Atlantic treaty and representing the principal political parties of such democracies, for the purpose of exploring how far their peoples, and the peoples of such other democracies as the convention may invite to send delegates, can apply among them, within the framework of the United Nations, the principles of federal union.
He said': Mr. Speaker,
The people of the earth having agreed
that the advancement of man in spiritual excellence and physical welfare
is the common goal of mankind; that universal peace is the prerequisite
for the pursuit of that goal;
that justice in turn is the prerequisite of peace, and peace and justice stand or fall together;
that iniquity and war inseparably spring
from the competitive anarchy of the national states; that therefore the age of nations must end,
and the era of humanity begin;
the governments of the nations have decided
to order their separate sovereignties
in one government of justice, to which they surrender their arms;
and to establish, as they do establish, this constitution
as the covenant and fundamental law
of the Federal Republic of the World.
There is the end, the goal, the ideal which I am certain is in the minds and hearts of all. The words which I have quoted are taken from the preamble of a draft constitution for world government. This draft constitution was prepared by a committee of eleven very distinguished men who met for a period of at least two years. Its chairman was Mr. Robert M. Hutchins, then president of Chicago university, and one of its members was Professor Harold Innis of the university of Toronto. The purpose of such a federation, such a world government, can be stated quite clearly. It is to give man greater freedom and equality by making man subject to the rule of law. Its hope is to abolish
the scourge of war. Its hope is to give the children of the world that security which our parents have denied us.
It envisages world union, which is something devoutly to be wished for but which today, owing' to the nature of things, is obviously utterly impossible. The words which I use in the resolution, while they express hope for a modified form of union, should not be new to members of the house for they are substantially the same as those which were accepted by the Canadian Senate last year. They are substantially the same as those words which today are before the houses of congress in the United States.
What I am asking is that approval be given to the suggestion that the sponsor nations of the North Atlantic treaty organization ask representatives from each of the major political parties to meet to discuss the possibility of forming some type of union such as I envisage. It is not restrictive, for its members would have the right to ask others, but with this aspect of restriction I shall deal later and more fully. Nothing which I have to say will be original; nothing will be new. All these things have been said before but the fact that they have been said before does not in any way invalidate them. It will be asked: What do I expect of such a union? The first and most obvious thing is that there should be a common citizenship with a bill of rights protecting the individual, for the individual is the very heart and core of any system of union such as I have in mind.
Not only would it do that but it would also protect the rights of minorities in the nations which are members of the union. To take our own country, for instance, I am convinced there would be no infringement whatsoever upon the rights of any individual or any minority. Rather I think through union would those inalienable rights be strengthened.	,
I would expect to see a common foreign policy. It may be argued that we have a common foreign policy now. We democratic nations of the North Atlantic are determined that we shall not be aggressors at any time. We are determined that peace shall ensue through the maintenance of law and order. It is true we have a common policy to that effect. Yet there are differences between us, differences which are perhaps not so great as many of us fear but differences which in a world of sovereign states must be dangerous, and under a union I think many of those differences would not be so apparent. We would need to have a common defence policy.

Federal Union
Today as sovereign nations we are arming against the threat of aggression. Sovereign nations in. the past, the nations of the north Atlantic and others, have indulged in an arms race when they thought it necessary for their own defence. They have entered into alliances and treaties. They have sought bases for their greater individual security. Yet history shows that treaties, leagues and covenants never kept sovereign states together. History also shows that the ally of yesteryear may well be the enemy of next year.
In a world of sovereign states there are three ways of solving problems, by the overwhelming bludgeoning of force, by negotiation or by war, but in a world of sovereign states when all else has failed the only way in which a nation can insist on its rights is by that extraordinarily stupid way of going to war. Again it may be argued that we already have a common defence under way but it is something which is only in the embryonic stage. Should the commander in chief of the allied forces, General Eisenhower, wish to expend any large sum of money for the common defence of all, he has to go before the council of twelve. Each of these individuals must go back to his national government and there get approval or disapproval for the projected expenditure. Today, when war may strike with the speed of lightning, such a procedure is slow and cumbersome and may conceivably lull us into a false sense of security. Under union the commander in chief would have power to decide, subject to the parliament of the union, what was needed; and that parliament then would vote him the money. This would imply that the union must have the power to impose taxation and collect taxes. I suspect that were our defences pooled in the union we should find taxes for defence not quite so onerous as they are upon us now as citizens of an individual state.
I would envisage also a free movement of peoples and goods. As a result of the greatly enlarged area of free trade, obviously there would be a rapid improvement in the standard of living of all. I am convinced that there are Canadian manufacturers and workers who believe that if tariffs were to be removed immediately the effect upon Canada might well be devastating. On the other hand, however, there is an argument which might appeal to them. By abolishing these tariffs we would open a new market of some three hundred million people. In the past we have learned to our cost that insistence upon our own sovereignty has led only too often to economic autarchy and a decline in the standard of living which of necessity must follow.

There is another factor which I think has to be borne in mind today. Industry in the western world is extraordinarily efficient and tremendously productive, so much so that the individual state has become too small a unit in which it may operate. So it would be the better part of wisdom to adapt our institutions to the new society which is being formed before our very eyes. If we are to have the free movement of goods and peoples it follows, surely, that we must have a common currency; and I am certain that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) would be the first to agree that national currencies have been one of the greatest deterrents to trade this world has ever known.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE AS TO APPLICATION OF PRINCIPLE BY DEMOCRACIES WITHIN UNITED NATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the dinner recess I was outlining to the house my idea as to the form which union should take. There is nothing sacred about these views of mine. Many who agree, as I do, on the necessity for union, would possibly disagree with me quite strongly on some details. Nevertheless I offer my suggestions as a basis for discussion. Now what would we hope to achieve out of union? The first and most obvious objectives would be the establishment of a great commonwealth of free peoples dedicated to the spiritual and physical freedom of mankind; and the achievement of a union which might be strong enough to deter an aggressor from any military action against us. What weighs largely in my mind is this fact. If a war were to come, if we are to fight it efficiently and effectively, we should find ourselves in a union such as I have suggested, whether we liked it or not. But while I welcome the idea of union, I should prefer to see it created when we have time to think about what we are doing and the problems we are facing rather than have it done under the duress of war.
In June of 1940, when things were black indeed for our cause, Mr. Churchill offered to the people of France common citizenship with the people of the United Kingdom. He offered them this as a means of salvation in a time of extremity. Unhappily, the time was too late. Today we are not in a moment of extremity, it is true. We have time to think of what we are doing and I still believe that our salvation lies in the direction of union.

From the more material point of view we can argue that union, of the western democracies with certain other nations would mean that we have amongst ourselves some 75 per cent of the industrial capacity of the world. It is true that, in the final analysis, it is the infantry, the men in our defence forces, who win wars. But no matter how great their heroism or how outstanding their courage, if they cannot get the arms with which to fight it is of no avail. Wars today are won in factories and really nowhere else. What we have to remember is that it is the first battle we have to win this time. In the past we have prided ourselves on always having won the last battle. But on this occasion, if war comes, the first battle will be that for Europe; and if we lose Europe, then the outlook for us on the North American continent will be bleak and grim indeed.
I said earlier that the union which I envisaged should not be exclusive. We should work with partners, with people whose human values are the same as ours, whose regard for human personality is the same as ours and who have the same desire for freedom. Indeed, the strongest of all possible bases for union would be a common allegiance to the democratic forms of government to which we adhere.
Again the question may be asked: Would this rule out Asia? At first I should be inclined to say no. But on second thought I would qualify the answer. We are convinced here, as are many people in Asia, that communism cannot help that continent. Yet our answers have not contained really adequate and convincing solutions. It is true we fight for freedom. But then, we know what freedom is. Tens of millions of people in Asia do not know what freedom is. Instead they have lives in which they have to endure unending hunger, lives of hopeless poverty, lives which too often are short and brutal; and what is worst of all, they have to suffer from the wretched indignity of being looked upon as being inferior people because their skins are coloured.
We ought to remember that Asia today is not in revolt against the Soviet union. Asia is in revolt against the western world and against the imperialism which it associates with it. I think that much of that imperialism is disappearing. Nevertheless, it is that which Asians fear. I should therefore like to see in this commonwealth of free people the citizens of India, Pakistan and Ceylon. I should like to see them in it for this reason, if for none other; and to my mind it is predominant. As a member of the Christian community I believe that the citizens of these countries are as we are, the children of God. That
Federal Union
being so, I affirm with them a common brotherhood. But union, as I see it, would be restricted for it would be manifestly absurd to enter into a union of this description with a totalitarian power. The very essence of union is its ability to appeal to the individual citizen. It would be the individual citizen who would appoint and elect his representatives to the union government; and since in a dictatorship we cannot reach the individual citizens, we need not be surprised if they would not apply for membership.
It is interesting to note that the desire for union springs not from the totalitarian countries but from the free citizens of the free nations. This is not a target for tomorrow. After all, tomorrow never comes. It is a target for today, for now. There are those who will say that my ideas are visionary. That may well be so. Yet surely the problems confronting the world today are not of necessity political nor are they of necessity economic problems; they are essentially moral problems, and we have not yet even started to find the answers. The realist, the one who prides himself on being hardheaded, may say that this is visionary; but there have been those of that ilk in other generations in the last two thousand years who have always believed that what Jesus Christ taught was excellent-but visionary. Nevertheless, if we had carried out a little more of what He taught, there would be no need for such a resolution before this parliament. There are those who say that the dangers of union are great. Of course the dangers of union are great, but the hopes which will arise from it are surely infinitely greater. There are difficulties ahead of us; there are incredible difficulties. But what impresses me most is that if a war does come these difficulties will be swept away, and I still argue it is better that we should unite now rather than under the stress and strain of war. As Mr. Churchill said at Copenhagen last year:
Unless a world government can be set up and brought quickly into action the prospects for peace and human progress are dark and doubtful.
Mr. Bevin said a little while ago that he was willing to sit with anybody, of any party, of any nation, to try to devise a constitution for a world assembly. And yet they know these difficulties. What are they? Some of them exist solely in the minds of people; and one of the greatest we have to combat is that of the concept of national sovereignty. Six years ago in the house in my first appearance in a debate on external affairs I used words that I believe to be true today. I said that national sovereignty is a fetish; it is a myth; it does not exist.

Federal Union
There cannot be one member of parliament who willingly voted or will vote for $5 billion for arms who would not rather spend that money on improving the conditions of people in this country and in other nations, and yet despite our sovereignty we are compelled to do so for our own protection. We have no alternative.
In other days our national sovereignty did not protect us against changes in tariff rates and currency devaluations, for we had to do precisely the same things as others to safeguard ourselves, although in the end we hurt ourselves. National sovereignty did not save us in 1939 when freedom was endangered. Today all over the world the lights of freedom are flickering and going out. Every time that freedom disappears in one part of the world it is going to affect us. We have realized that. As Archibald MacLeish, the then librarian of congress, said:
There has been destroyed in the minds of men and women in this country the superstition that what is done beyond three thousand miles of water is not really done at all; the ignorant superstition that violence and lies and murder on another continent are not violence and lies and murder here; the cowardly and brutal superstition that the enslavement of man in a country where the sun rises at midnight by our clock is not enslavement by the time we live by; the black and stifling superstition that what we cannot see and hear and touch can have no meaning for us.
We have our sovereignty. Nations of the world have insisted on sovereignty, and the result has been insecurity and anarchy. I want to substitute law and order for this anarchy, and let there be no illusions as to what I mean; for in this context I say that law is the justified use of force. Law exists only where there is force. Law exists only where there is coercive power. There must be force, and yet so many of us shrink from this idea. We regard it as something wrong, as something immoral, and yet force is a reality which can be used not only for great ends but for mean and ignoble ends. We are determined to use force to preserve those things which we cherish.
Then, what about this talk of peace? Peace as such is not important. Peace is an end result. We had peace in the 1930's; we had peace when Manchuria was invaded; we had peace when Ethiopia was ravaged; we had peace when Austria disappeared; we had peace when Czechoslovakia was submerged. We had peace when millions of human beings were being destroyed because of their faith and their religion. What sort of peace was it? The peace we knew was something unjust, uneasy and suspicious, which could only end in war. So it is advisable for us to institute law and order, and out of that peace must come. We have to face up to the

paradox of this century, namely, that to preserve peace we have to be ready to use force.
We have learned the folly of sovereignty surely in our own individual lives. Each of us has given up his personal sovereignty to the community in which he resides, and as a result of that denial we find ourselves freer than ever. We have security; we have equality of rights where otherwise there would be chaos.
We have surrendered our sovereignty to the community so that it can administer law and order and punish the law breaker and the aggressor. Life would be intolerable if each of us insisted on retaining his sovereignty. We would walk in fear and trembling as to what was going to happen to us. Each of us would be armed to the teeth and we should see that anarchy in our private lives, which as individuals we have forsworn, but which we are still prepared to accept in our international lives.
The same thing is true of civic and provincial sovereignty. We have surrendered to our country, Canada, certain rights concerning the defence of the nation, the trade and commerce of the nation, the banking and currency, the foreign policy of the nation, and as a result of that surrender we find that all of us are stronger, and each of us is freer.
There may be in the minds of some the idea that a greater union would betoken some disloyalty on our part. I dispute that. My loyalty to my family does not weaken my loyalty to Canada. My loyalty to my church does not infringe upon my loyalty to Canada. .My loyalty to the city from which I come does not decrease my loyalty to Canada. Instead it is part of the greater loyalty.
Of course there are those who will fear we are merely building a superstate; but not if you accept my premise of union founded on the individual citizen. The individual citizen will elect his representatives to the union government, composed of a bicameral legislature, I presume. Thus you will see that no superstate is envisaged, for the individual is paramount. All that we will surrender will be these things which will lead to our greater safety, our greater welfare when done collectively. Nor do I see any conflict with the United Nations charter. The United Nations unhappily is essentially an instrument of diplomacy. It cannot give us that security which we want in this world, and as an indication of that certain of us have joined the North Atlantic treaty organization so we can have a greater security. I believe that this union could be a member of the United Nations without infringing upon the charter of that organization at all.

A greater argument, a more valid one, is that the citizens of North America might not be willing to surrender part of their standard of living to other peoples; but I retort again that if a war comes they will have to surrender part of that standard of living, and the people of the United States have been doing it through the Marshall plan, as we to some modified extent shall be doing it through the Colombo plan.
Earlier 1 said there were material things which we could achieve. There is something greater which we can achieve. There are spiritual achievements awaiting us. Today the morale of Europe is not nearly as high as we should like it to be. There is a sense of defeatism in certain areas, a desire for neutralism, a desire not to fight but rather to live no matter under what circumstances. I believe that if we were to offer these people, who are our potential allies, this concept of union, then Europe would be stirred to its depths by the fervour which made liberty, equality and fraternity a battlecry which resounded all around this world. We should find that fear would give place to hope, doubt would be replaced by certainty, and indecision by decision. We could once again rekindle the flickering lamps of their faith. Here would be the sort of leadership which the souls of men the world over today are groping for. As Walter Reuther said:
The best chance of saving freedom and achieving peace is in an action so challenging, so vast in scope, so practical in design and so sincere in purpose that it fills the moral vacuum in the world with new and with reborn hope.
There are still those who will say it is not possible. My answer is in the words of a French general in the first world war: C'est impossible; done faisons-le.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of Slate for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE AS TO APPLICATION OF PRINCIPLE BY DEMOCRACIES WITHIN UNITED NATIONS
speechtext:
Mir. Speaker, I feel I should say a few words about this resolution which has been moved in such eloquent terms by the hon. member who has just taken his seat. I should say at once that I support, and I think the government supports, the purposes and principles and the idealism which underlie this resolution. But I am not myself certain that those purposes could best be achieved or those principles best implemented by the procedure recommended in the resolution.
As has been pointed out, the resolution requests the government to "take into consideration the advisability of supporting the calling of a convention of delegates from the democracies which sponsored the North Atlantic treaty and representing the principal
Federal Union
political parties of such democracies, for the purpose of exploring how far their peoples, and the peoples of such other democracies as the convention may invite to send delegates, can apply among them, within the framework of the United Nations, the principles of federal union."
The meaning of the resolution, then, is quite clear. It is interesting to note that a resolution in almost these same terms was discussed in Washington-last June, I believe it was-and also in the autumn of 1950, by the Senate of the United States. A resolution in these terms, or in terms very similar to this resolution, has also been discussed in the other place, here.
The discussion in Washington resulted in no decision being taken at that time by the government of the United States. But a report on this very important matter was made by a Senate subcommittee of the Senate foreign relations committee, which set out very clearly and very effectively the pros and cons on action of this kind.
The administration in Washington, however, has expressed its views already on this matter; and possibly it might be of interest to the house if I read from a statement made before the Senate subcommittee by the assistant secretary of state of the United States in which he gives the administration's point of view on the question. At that time, February 15, 1950, the administration's point of view was expressed by their spokesman, the assistant secretary of state, Mr. Hickerson, as follows:
We believe-
That is, the United States government.
-that progressively closer association, by limited and practicable steps on the basis of common interests, and in support of the purposes and principles of the United Nations, within as much as practicable of the free world, is both necessary and desirable.
And then he went on to say:
In the development of such closer association, care must be exercised not to set in motion forces which will render more difficult the maintenance of the solidarity of the free world in support of the principles and purposes of the United Nations.
In a number of countries in the Atlantic community progress in both the national and international fields has resulted from the willingness of certain groups to accept sacrifices primarily on the basis of national interest. It will take a very long time before similar strong loyalty to a new political unit emerges. We believe-
He said,
-that under the present North Atlantic treaty arrangements we are utilizing this force in the most constructive way at this stage of development in international relations. The establishment at this time of such a federation-
As is proposed in this resolution.
-far from providing additional strength, could be a source of weakness and greater internal divisions.

Federal Union
Furthermore, the effective operation of democracy in some of the suggested participants is severely hampered by the system of splinter parties which might be carried over and even intensified in such a federation.
And then he ended in this way:
The proposed resolution-
That is, the American resolution.
-directs its attention primarily to calling a convention to explore the possibilities of Atlantic union. We believe that if the government should sponsor such a convention at this time it would raise false hopes. If the convention did not succeed it would lead to reactions unfavourable to the cause of collective security. Under present circumstances such a convention appears more likely to bring to light and emphasize the divisions among the proposed members of the Atlantic union than to lead to substantial progress in the desired direction. In view of these facts the projected convention would seem likely to weaken rather than to strengthen both the Atlantic community and the United Nations.
That, Mr. Speaker, remains, as I understand it, the attitude of the United States government toward a development of this kind. I think it is quite clear that without at least the co-operation of, and I would hope in this case possibly leadership by, the United States government, it is not likely to be practicable to convene a convention of the kind indicated in the resolution.
I am not suggesting for one moment, nor would I want to give the impression, that we disagree with the principle embodied in the resolution, or that we would minimize in any way the necessity in the present dangerous international situation of the closest possible kind of international cooperation among all the nations of the free world-not only the seven supporting nations under the Atlantic treaty. I would not take my stand for one moment in respect of a resolution of this kind on the desirability or essentiality of unrestricted national sovereignty.
National sovereignty has played its part- its very important and constructive part-in building up the nation-state out of feudalism, and in progress toward democratic liberty and social advancement. But I agree with the ion. member who has just spoken that we are living in an age today different from that in which national sovereignty emerged. We are living in an age, not so much of independence, important though that may be, as of interdependence. It would be, not only unwise, it might even be disastrous, if we clung to any barren, negative, legalistic interpretation of national sovereignty. Why, every time we sign a treaty with some other country we give up some part of our national sovereignty-or, as I prefer to put it, we are making our sovereignty work for us in the interests of peace and security by pooling

our sovereignty with other like-minded states; so that by giving something up we get more.
As I see it, there is no possibility of preserving peace or establishing security by basing our policy on any legal, narrow interpretation of national sovereignty. So if I have hesitation about this resolution, and I have, it is not because I am clinging to that, in some respects, and some respects only, outworn ideal. It would not be of much help to us in this country if we lost everything else and saved our sovereignty.
I think that this process from the single nation state based on the Austinian theory of legal sovereignty to groups of interdependent states is an important one and should go forward. It is going forward every month and every year. If this development is to be effective however, if it is to be constructive, I suggest that it must be gradual and not get too far in advance of public opinion in the various nation states of the world who would become part of any such federation as that which is visualized in this resolution.
Further, a world federation, such a Tenny-sonian concept, if I may call it that, is not an end in itself, but merely the means to an end. That end is peace and international co-operation. A federation itself is not any assurance that these ends will be met, either internationally or even domestically. The belief that federations inevitably prevent war domestically was shattered finally, I should think, in 1861 in the United States. The choice before us is not between federation and survival but between collective action and survival. I am not sure that in the present circumstances the latter is not even easier without forcing the former.
Certainly the problems inherent in international co-operation would not be exorcised by taking our stand on anything like federal union, especially a federal union where power would be so unevenly divided between the dominant United States and a country like Luxembourg. I think our own commonwealth of nations offers the best example I can think of international co-operation on the closest intimate basis without federal institutions or without federal union of any kind being found to be necessary. As a matter of fact if we had had to institutionalize our co-operation within the commonwealth that co-operation might not be as close as it is today.
So there are difficulties in the way of carrying out an advance of this kind, because it would be an advance, If we do not understand those difficulties and if we plunge headlong into a conference of this kind without

Federal Union
understanding them, we might very well find that far from having made progress we would have set back the wheels of progress. Some of the questions which would come before any convention of this kind leap automatically to one's mind. How far would the people of the various countries go in altering their own form of government and accepting the basic economic and social changes which must inevitably follow through the federation? For instance, how far would they go in 1951 in giving up control over exports, imports, currency, taxation, finance and immigration?
A constitutional convention of the type visualized in this resolution, if it did anything at all, would have to deal with these matters at once. I suggest that in doing so it would raise far more problems than it would solve. It would raise hopes which could not in the nature of things be realized at this time. It might be followed by disappointment and disillusionment which would set back rather than advance the cause of closer union and more intimate co-operation.
A convention of this kind might even cause among the free nations which would be invited to it confusion and division and possibly even disunity. Far from assisting in the move toward federation itself, a premature attempt at this time might set it back. The hon. member who has just spoken has pointed out that in the first instance a convention of this kind would include only the seven powers that have sponsored the Atlantic charter. As he pointed out, it is true that provision could be made for inviting other countries to attend later.
The seven sponsoring powers are the United States, the United Kingdom, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg and Canada. We would inevitably run into difficulties when we began to pick and choose other powers to join us in this constitutional convention. That kind of discussion in a convention of that kind would not, as I see it, be conducive now to achieving the ends which are desired by us and which are expressed in this resolution.
I think it might be particularly confusing at this time to have a convention of this nature because of the steps that are being taken and the progress that has been made already in Europe toward a federation of European states. Very important discussions with far-reaching consequences are taking place looking toward European union and the creation of European machinery. While those discussions are important and I think filled with hope, they have indicated already some of the difficulties in the way of even a European federation. To superimpose at this
time on those discussions the wider discussion of an Atlantic federation, or a federation even wider than the Atlantic, would not I think be helpful toward the very important movement which has developed in the way of European unity.
I pay a sincere tribute to the idea behind this resolution which I think we all hope will be realized one day, but I do not think to associate ourselves at this time with such a hypothetical invitation would be well advised. There is one further difficulty which I have not mentioned, the relationship of the commonwealth countries to a convention of this kind. Would they all be included, or would only some be included? If only some were included, would not that mean a possible weakening of the links between all the commonwealth countries?
I think I should mention to the house that this question is now once again before the United States congress in its current session. A few weeks ago the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) received a letter from Senator Guy M. Gillette. He was writing on behalf of a number of senators who are sponsoring a resolution of this kind before the senate. I am not going to read the whole letter but I should like to read a couple of paragraphs from it. It is addressed to our Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and is dated January 24, 1951. In its opening paragraph it refers to the resolution now before the United States senate. Senator Gillette goes on to say about that resolution that it represents-and I am quoting from the letter:
... an effort to improve upon our first essay in Atlantic collaboration. It proposes that the original seven sponsors of the North Atlantic treaty send delegates to a convention to explore how far the Atlantic community is willing to go in merging its political, diplomatic, military and economic resources for the common good.
In that sense it is almost the same kind of resolution we have before us this evening. Then Senator Gillette ends his letter as follows:
Some of us are engaged in forming, among members of the United States congress, an informal committee to advance this exploratory effort. It would be of great value if you would inform us how far your views on ways and means of meeting the present crisis accord with those set forth above and whether you would be prepared to form a similar group within your parliamentary body.
The Prime Minister replied to that letter on January 31, as follows:
Dear Senator Gillette:
I duly received your letter of January 24, regarding the concurrent resolution standing in the name of Senator Kefauver, yourself and a number of your colleagues, calling for exploration of the possibilities of forming an Atlantic union.
I think you will appreciate how embarrassing it might be for both countries if the head of the

Federal Union
government of one of our countries were to express himself about the content or efficacy of a specific proposal which was under consideration in the other country, and on which a conclusion had not been reached. You may be assured, however, that should the resolution pass and the president carry out the request contained therein, it would receive the most careful consideration of the Canadian government.
As for the possibility of forming a similar group in the Canadian parliament, and particularly in the House of Commons, this is something which it would not be possible, because of our different constitutional structure, for the head of the administration to sponsor, unless and until the policy proposed had become a definite policy of the administration. Since the success of the proposal contained in your resolution would clearly depend upon the initiative being taken by the United States government, it would, I feel, be premature for our administration to take any initiative until a decision had been reached in principle in Washington. That, of course, would not preclude the advocacy of similar proposals by private members of our parliament; as was the case in respect of the resolution considered in our Senate last year.
I regret that I cannot be more specific in my reply, but I can assure you and your colleagues in the United States senate that any action which will have the practical effect of strengthening the North Atlantic community will, I believe, meet with a favourable response in Canada.
Before I sit down I should like to point out to the house that action is already being taken to strengthen the north Atlantic community under the North Atlantic pact. It does not go as far of course as this resolution would have us go, and progress may not be as fast or as far as some of us would like, but progress is being made in implementing article 2, for instance, of the North Atlantic treaty. Effective liaison arrangements have been worked out between members of the North Atlantic group in economic matters- especially, I admit, economic matters concerned with defence. The North Atlantic treaty organization and the OEEC have established effective working relationships, and indeed I think it may not be going too far to say that some of the economic functions which are now being performed by the office of European economic co-operation will be taken over by the North Atlantic treaty organization. We are also discussing the building up under the North Atlantic organization of a permanent international secretariat. So we are making some progress at this time under the North Atlantic organization toward the development of a north Atlantic community. I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that at this time that is the most effective way by which we can work towards achievement of the fine objective put forward in this resolution.
I said not very long ago "that our North Atlantic alliance may provide the foundation for a great co-operative economic commonwealth of the western world which one day may become a political commonwealth. You may say that this is unrealistic nonsense but

I suggest that in this jet-propelled atomic age no plan less than this will be adequate, no vision less than this will do." So far as I am concerned I stand by those words, but I do not think that at this time the calling of a conference of the type indicated by the resolution would make any appreciable advance to the attainment of the ultimate objective, which remains a commonwealth of the free world. Therefore, in order that we in this house may not give the appearance of division and disunity on a matter as to which we are all fundamentally united, I would venture to express the hope that this resolution may not be pressed to a vote at this time.

subtopic: DECENTRALIZATION TO ENSURE MORE BALANCED ECONOMY AND PROVIDE PROTECTION IN TIME OF WAR

speakeroldname: Mr. Clarence Gillis (Cape Breton South) moved:
subtopic: DECENTRALIZATION TO ENSURE MORE BALANCED ECONOMY AND PROVIDE PROTECTION IN TIME OF WAR
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to a program for the decentralization of industry, so as to make possible a more balanced economy and for protection in the event of war.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the subject matter of the resolution is one that has been raised on a good many occasions in this house, generally by way of interjection into a debate where no definite expression of opinion could be had. I thought it was advisable at this time to place this resolution on the order paper for the purpose not only of having a definite discussion of the matter but also of getting a decision in the house by way of a vote as to what, in the opinion of hon. members, is the solution of the difficulties that I am going to attempt to set out. At the outset I want to say that I do not believe in introducing a resolution for the purpose of getting a discussion, and then withdrawing it. It is either worth getting a decision on or it is not worth putting on the order paper.
The question of decentralization of industry in Canada has occupied the minds and attention of a great many people. The premier of Ontario made a statement at the last dominion-provincial conference on December 4 to 7, 1950. I am not going to read that statement, which appears on pages 21, 22, 23 and 24 of the report, but in it he set out that the great centralization of industry in Ontario

had brought this province additional problems and responsibilities they were finding it rather difficult to handle at the present time. Industry was concentrated in this province from 1940 to 1949 to such an extent that a terrific power shortage developed, and the province had to embark upon a power program that is taxing its financial resources. In addition a labour problem was created, and as a result they not only had to bring in labour from other provinces but were thinking of importing labour from overseas in order to complete their power program. There were also problems in connection with the expansion of hospital services, medical services and other services of that kind. In effect I would read into the statement of the premier a plea to those now responsible for the planning of additional expansion in this country for greater equalization all across the country in order to relieve Ontario and Quebec of many of the social problems created by the overexpansion of industry in these central provinces.
I have dug up a few figures. First I want to say, however, that this is not a problem that developed only last year or the year before. I am going to speak particularly of the maritimes, though the western provinces are in pretty much the same position, and I expect western members to speak for them. I would point out that the trend towards centralization in Ontario and Quebec has not . changed very much in the last twenty years. In my opinion the difficulty arose sixty years ago or more, and I should like to call the attention of hon. members to a few very pertinent facts.
At confederation the maritime provinces were the richest part of this country; there is no disputing that fact. When Nova Scotia and the maritimes came into confederation they were given certain definite promises by way of maritime rights. The idea of confederation was that we were building one nation, and there was to be greater opportunity to expand the industries, and develop the resources of the maritimes through the creation of a great central market for those provinces. Let me point out what happened in the field of finance. At the time of confederation we had in Nova Scotia the Merchants Bank, the Bank of Nova Scotia, the Halifax Banking Company, the Bank of Yarmouth, the Commercial Bank of Windsor and the Union Bank of Halifax. All these banks were staffed by Nova Scotians. They were handling Nova Scotia capital, using the finances of the province for the purpose of building up commerce and industry there. After confederation all these banks disappeared; they moved west and were centralized in Quebec and Ontario. In that
Decentralization of Industry way Nova Scotia lost control of her own finances. Instead of the capital which was siphoned off and taken into the central provinces being used to promote commerce and industry in the maritime provinces, it was used to bring about the centralization we have today in Ontario and Quebec. We lost control of our finances, and we lost our ability to promote industry and commerce in the maritimes.
That was strike one against confederation. Now let me go through a list of some of the industries we lost at that time. We had a cotton mill in Halifax, for the information of the senior member for Halifax. We also had a cotton mill at Windsor. We had a paint works at Halifax, three tobacco factories, five shoe factories, two soap factories and three woollen mills. We had a cheese factory at Antigonish that won a prize at a world's fair several decades ago, and a condensed milk factory at Truro. At Sydney we had a fertilizer plant and a large tar and chemical works. These industries have all disappeared. If you read Norman Rogers' economic survey, which can be obtained in the library, you will find that up to 1935 the maritime provinces had lost some 202 industries to the central provinces.
I said the trend had not changed very much in the last twenty years. I have the figures here showing the 1929 gross production by provinces on a percentage basis, and they were as follows:

There has been a shift of about five per cent in the gross production of the country as between Quebec and Ontario and the rest of the country, but that shift has gone to British Columbia. That province has benefited by this swing, and I think that is because of the increase in population. The point I am trying to make clear is that the inequalities as between province and province in this country were fixed back about fifty years ago. Everything possible was siphoned off and centralized, including finance, industry and so forth. There has not been in the last twenty-five years any attempt on the part of the government or on the part of private industry in this country to rectify that situation. It has remained practically stationary. What I am trying to prove to the government is this. That is what has taken place in the past. There is not much use in holding a post mortem. But there is no reason why we should not take a look at the matter for a minute or two in order to show that there has been an extremely unequal distribution of the wealth of this country as between province and province. There is no indication that that 66 per cent concentration of the manufacturing and of the gross production of this country that is centred in those two provinces is justified by population trends. It certainly is not.
During the last war the government had the chance of planning their defence production in such a way as to leave in the various provinces some industry that could be utilized for peacetime purposes. All during the last war, while the government was going into their defence program, we on this side of the house argued and argued that we should at least decentralize our defence production to the greatest possible extent and that we should decide on the plants we would establish, having in mind the fact that the population of this country was going to be increased to a greater and greater extent by immigration. That is also true of the future.
[Mr. Gillis.l

We are starting in again to plan a huge defence program. It means not only swinging over a certain percentage of the plants that are now in production but it also means that the basic steel industry, for example, will have to be expanded. The logical place to expand the basic steel industry is in Nova Scotia. There is no arguing against that statement. Most of our defence planning at this time is to equip our allies overseas. Those who are taking part in the North Atlantic pact defence program are our allies for the future and will be for a long time to come. Our major contribution in that field is going to be the supplying to them of guns, munitions and vehicles of war. If we are going to ship that material overseas, what is the logical place to ship it from if we are not thinking in terms of profits and dollars for General Motors, Chrysler and some of those people? If we are really honest about wanting to make our maximum contribution with the least possible expense to the taxpayers of Canada, the place to produce guns and steel and what-have-you is where you have your raw materials and where you have your largest unemployed force in Canada today. Do not forget what Uncle Sam is doing. Two, three and four years ago I rose in my place in this house and argued about this iron ore development. We passed a bill here handing over the iron ore deposits of Labrador and Ungava to Hol-linger and these holding companies in Canada but with the main direction over in the United States. We passed a bill here by which we gave them the right to take over the iron ore deposits and develop them; and now we sit back and talk about expanding the steel industry down in Hamilton. Is it not rather a ridiculous thing, if you stop and think about it for a minute? One-third of Canada's basic steel is produced down there in Sydney, Nova Scotia. Right across the water, ninety miles away at Wabana, the iron ore is there. Thirteen miles away they have unlimited supplies of good steelmaking coal, where your unemployed lists are the greatest of any in any part of the country, and those boys are steelmakers or coal producers. They fit right into that picture logically, but they are walking the streets. Is it logical to suppose that we turn out that raw steel and haul it all the way up to Ontario and Quebec to have it processed? Do not forget that you pay a subsidy on hauling that raw material up across Canada. Then when it is processed and you have turned it into guns or vehicles, you haul them all the way back again to Halifax or down to Sydney- because that is where they are shipped from1-put them on a boat and ship them over to Europe. All during the last war at
69$

least two hundred ships a day went in and out of Sydney harbour, making the crossing back and forth across the Atlantic. Let us save that two-way rail haul this time. Let us establish a plant or two down there. Let us expand the steelmaking facilities down there.
I pick up the newspapers every day and note that the Americans are decentralizing their steelmaking industry in the United States. They are shifting their plants down to the states of Maine and New Hampshire. Down on the Atlantic seaboard they have routed in or are in the process of routing in four different big plants. We said that two years ago. We said that there was going to be a major shift in the basic steel plants in the United States. That is why we wanted to hang on to our iron ore deposits. But we did not manage to do that. The Americans have control of that ore. Now they want the seaway opened up. Two hundred and forty million dollars will be Canada's share of opening up that seaway to give them access to that raw material in Labrador, which they will haul up there by boat, by-pass your eastern ports altogether and in the future they will be supreme in steel on this North American continent. We had it in our hands to be supreme but we did not take advantage of the opportunity. We passed the charters on to somebody else who will do the exploiting. I am making a plea at this time that the government look at this matter not just as a two-year or three-year program, something that is going to be over when the war is over. I want the government at this time to see this as a program that is going to last for as long as we are going to last; because this defence business is something we are going to have for a good many years to come. Let us plan these industries in such a way that while they are of necessity now making war materials, we shall be able to convert that plant for the manufacture of something for the overseas market possibly, in that end of the country, in the years that lie ahead.
I am making a plea for the decentralization of industry as it exists today. In the event of war, if we have 66 per cent of our gross production concentrated in those two central provinces, what does it mean? It merely means this. If 26 per cent is in the province of Quebec, then about 24 per cent is on the island of Montreal. What could a plane with a couple of atomic bombs do by coming in over the island of Montreal and dropping them in there somewhere? What would happen? About 24 per cent of your gross production would be knocked out overnight. If you have 40 per cent of your gross production in the province of Ontario, where is
Decentralization of Industry it centred? There are only two or three places you have to hit; they are Hamilton, Windsor and Toronto. That is where your real manufacturing is done. If we mean what we say to the Canadian people, that they are going to be taxed higher, that they are going to have to pay a great deal more money, that we are going into a heavy defence program which is necessary, that there is danger of atomic attack on this continent, then we should start planning for that and start decentralizing to the greatest possible extent the industrial set-up of this country today.
I merely wanted to raise this question because in every paper I pick up some great economist-I do not bother reading them any more-has a long story, about professor somebody saying that the government is recognizing to the greatest possible extent the great wealth of the maritime provinces and telling what they are going to do to develop it. I have been listening to that sort of thing for the last fifty years, but it just finishes up by being a speech; that is all, nothing is ever done about it. The steel workers' union come and present a brief to the cabinet of Nova Scotia. They are demanding some expansion of steel in the maritime provinces and all that kind of stuff. The cabinet meets them and says "amen", the brief goes into the waste basket and that is the end of it. That sort of thing has been going on for the last fifty years. I thought it time that I should bring the matter before the house so that there could be a definite and specific discussion. I do not want the resolution withdrawn. I want hon. members to discuss it. I want the cabinet, which is responsible in the years that lie ahead for planning our production, both for defence and internal economy, to tell me what they mean when they say that they recognize the great potentialities of the maritimes. I want to know what they are going to do about it. What are they going to do to restore the 202 industries that have been siphoned off? For example, take fertilizer: one of the largest plants ever developed in this country was at Sydney, Nova Scotia. It employed 1,700 people. In the 1930's it was siphoned off and came up to Toronto. Today that plant is manufacturing fertilizer and shipping it down to the farmers of Nova Scotia at a cost of about $90 a ton, and the federal government is paying most of the freight rates on it. It would have been better if that plant had stayed there, and that goes for a lot of other things that have left the maritime provinces.
One member of the cabinet not so long ago indicated that he was getting a little tired
696	HOUSE OF
Decentralization of Industry of listening to people of the maritime provinces bringing their complaints. It is not a complaint; it is not a request for charity; it is a matter of restoring the things that belong to that part of the country that were siphoned off because the provincial leaders were honest enough to accept the word of the fathers of confederation that they were coming into confederation for the purpose of developing a country where there would be greater opportunities for their products in a central market. Instead of that tariff walls were built to protect the manufacturers of the central provinces. We have to buy in a wholly protected market, and we have to sell in that market. Yet there is absolutely no protection for what we produce in that end of the country.
I should like to see this matter discussed. I discuss it from the standpoint of a member from the maritime provinces. I see these same arguments that I am using for that end of the country applied to British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. They are not getting a square deal. I do not think it was ever envisaged by the fathers of confederation that 82 per cent of the gross production of this country should be centralized in two provinces, and that tariff walls to protect the manufacturers of those provinces should be built to the detriment of the rest of the country east and west.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DECENTRALIZATION TO ENSURE MORE BALANCED ECONOMY AND PROVIDE PROTECTION IN TIME OF WAR
speechtext:
I am sure we are all in sympathy with the objectives of the hon. member, but I am equally sure that there cannot be very many of us in sympathy with the arguments he used to try to reach those objectives. A few minutes ago he said that practically everything that had been going on for the last fifty years finished in speeches. Well, I think when the hon. member reads tomorrow what he said tonight he will find that there is more of a speech than anything constructive in what he has put before the house tonight. His last assertion was that tariff walls have been built around this country to protect the manufacturing interests of the central provinces. The tariff walls are walls that protect all the industries of the country wherever they are located, and those tariff walls were built a good many years ago.
In spite of that, what the hon. member refers to as a siphoning off of industries seems to have been taking place. He refers to one that was siphoned off from Sydney to Toronto in the 1930's. Well, I do not know how the siphoning process was brought about, but I am sure the hon. member is not suggesting that the government had anything to do with the siphoning off of the industry; that was something which was decided by those


who had control of the industry. Of course I admit that those who feel that these industries should be owned and administered by the state can complain of the way their owners, who operate under the profit system, are letting their interests influence the location of these industries.
But then the hon. member says that if less thought was given to profits for General Motors, Chrysler and the others, some industrial expansion might take place in the maritime provinces. Well, if the investments are going to be made by General Motors, by Chrysler and by such other private enterprise groups, they will think of the profits to be made, and they will be apt to pick out for their plants such locations as are likely to produce the best returns on the investments made.
The hon. member says that there were 282 industries in the maritime provinces at the time of confederation-

Yet I do not think it was required to siphon off any that existed anywhere else in order to get them going in other localities.
The hon. member gave the figures for the national production in 1929. He said that of the total, Quebec then had 30 per cent and Ontario 52 per cent. He then gave figures for 1949, I think it was.

Well, in that period Quebec had 26 per cent and Ontario had 40 per cent. The two central provinces have thus fallen in those two decades from 82 per cent to 66 per cent, while according to the figures given there would have been practically no change in the proportion of the maritime provinces. Still there has been an increase from 14 per cent to 29 per cent for the four western provinces. That is something which certainly has not -siphoned off anything from the maritime provinces, but rather it is something that resulted from the growth and development of the country.
It would seem that the area of the maritime provinces being smaller and more contracted that that of the other provinces, their proportion, when the other provinces were less developed, was a larger one than it happened to be when the others came to grow. There has not been the same proportion of growth

in the maritime provinces as has taken place elsewhere, and it is something which we all regret, and about which perhaps many of us have been making speeches. I hope that more than speeches will be made, but I do not think the assertions that we find in the hon. member's speech tonight will bring that about.
He speaks of us as having handed over the iron ores of northeastern Quebec and Newfoundland to United States interests. Well, the hon. member knows, as I know, that natural resources are in no way under the control of the federal government. They are under the control of the provincial governments, and any handing over, if there has been any, has not been done here in this parliament, but by arrangements that have been entered into between provincial administrations and those who wanted to invest the venture capital required for the exploitation of those resources. Personally, as a resident of the province of Quebec, I have no complaint about the arrangements that have been made for the purpose of having those resources developed.
I remember when I was very much younger having heard violent criticism of a premier of Quebec who sold water power on the St. Maurice river for $13,000. It was a terrible scandal at that time; but no water power had been developed on the St. Maurice up to then. That was the first development and those who ventured into it found that it was years before they could be assured that they were ever going to get any return on their capital. Since then the development of water power on the St. Maurice has certainly become fifty times what it was originally. This first start was made some forty years ago.
I think this is very likely to be the case in the development of the mining resources of northeast Quebec, and over the frontier, the still undetermined frontier, between Newfoundland and Labrador. The existence of ores there has been known and reported for several decades, but nothing was done about it except that possibly, from time to time, some kind of a speech was made. Well someone is going in there at the present time, venturing huge sums, to demonstrate that there is something that can be used in the improvement of the conditions of human beings; and I think it is a very good thing that it should be done.
I know friends of mine have criticized the provincial administration for the kind of deal they made. But personally I am rather inclined to think that they are to be congratulated on having made a deal that has started something in that region. The hon. member says that as a consequence of this steelmakers in the United States are moving
Decentralization of Industry their plants to the Atlantic coast. Well, possibly steelmakers here, if they will have the courage to do what others have done in developing industries in Canada, will move Canadian steel plants to the Atlantic coast. It is being done by private enterprise in the United States; and I trust there will be sufficient enterprise among the people of Canada to bring them to do likewise.
I have frequently referred to the example of the governor and company of adventurers of England trading into Hudson bay as a very good example for our people to follow. Those gentlemen adventurers trading into Hudson bay went out into the wilds and created a trade which, before their adventure, had not existed. They laid the foundations of a company which, three centuries later, is still flourishing.
A century ago, perhaps a little more than that, progress was brought about in the Quebec district by gentlemen adventurers who were building wooden ships and sending them across the seven seas and throughout the world. And they did not come back- not because they were lost: they were good ships, and they were not lost. But they went into world trade and they stayed there.
Following that period the spirit of adventure seemed to diminish in our Quebec region. There were adventurers in Montreal who went out to build the railways and they had a pretty venturesome job ahead of them. They were frequently on the verge of losing everything or of seeing others lose everything in their ventures. But-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext: The government helped.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext:
They were assisted by
the government; and if they had not been assisted by the government my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) would not be here.
But their spirit of adventure then passed on to the city of Toronto. It was in the city of Toronto that the venture capital required to start our great mining industry, and to make it the important thing it has become, was raised and supplied.
Then, for the last few years I think many of us have somewhat regretted that the oil fields of Alberta had not attracted the same venture capital from Canadians that other industries had attracted; we regretted that most of the venture capital that went in there came from others who-I will not say "created", because the Creator himself put the oil there-but rather who brought it to the surface and are making it one of the very encouraging things in the whole Canadian economic picture at the present time.

Decentralization of Industry
Now, as my hon. friend says, we have heard about maritime rights ever since confederation. He tells me that at the time of confederation the maritime bankers were the great bankers of the British North American colonies. I have no doubt about that. The hon. member knows that in the administration of our banks all over Canada at the present time there are a great many maritimers who are descended from those bankers of preconfederation days. Private enterprise went to the fields that appeared to offer the best possibilities for getting revenue from investments-and I am sure there is no more prosperous bank in Canada today than the Bank of Nova Scotia. But the Bank of Nova Scotia, though it may technically still have its head office in Halifax-and I am not sure that it has-has its real head office, the office from which the affairs of the bank are administered from day to day, in central Canada. That is because the maritimers who controlled the institution felt that it was better for themselves and for their shareholders to have those operations conducted from Toronto.
Well, that is not something with which the government can interfere-until the government becomes imbued with the ideas of my hon. friends in that section of the house, and decides, with the approval of the Canadian people, that it is going to substitute some socialistic system for the private enterprise system, which has brought over the last couple of centuries such tremendous developments to the North American continent.
I think it is desirable to use all the influence we can to have these things spread out; and I wish to assure my hon. friend, without violating any cabinet secrets, that when these matters come before cabinet there are many who are most anxious to explore every angle by which greater dispersal of industry can be brought about, because, although we are living under a private enterprise system, we think it would be healthier for the country if industry were more widely spread out through all parts of the country. We think it would be healthier for the country if there was the teeming activity in the maritime provinces that would allow us to do away with such things, for instance, as maritime freight subsidies. We think it would be better for the country if that could be brought about, and we do give attention to it. We endeavour to use such influence as we have to that end.
I do not know anything about the making of steel; but I have heard it said that if and when the coal in the maritimes can be married to the kind of ore that would come from the Labrador mines, the steel industry of the maritime provinces would be in a much healthier condition. I do not know whether


that is so or not; but I do hear it said that the maritimes have been struggling against difficulties that came from, not the degree of skill of the men or the willingness of the men to work, but from the material they have to work with. I do not know if we are to infer from the hon. member's speech that he thinks it would not be desirable to have the St. Lawrence waterway and power scheme proceeded with. If that is to be inferred from his speech, I for one would disagree with him on that point. I think that if and when that undertaking is proceeded with, it will bring about a further advance in the industrial development of this country which will benefit, not only the central provinces but the economy of the whole nation.
If there were not in this motion submitted by the hon. member the implication that the government is to blame for not having done enough I am sure that everyone would be in agreement with the desirability of there being a greater dispersal of industry throughout the whole nation. But it is put forward as a condemnation of what has been going on in the past and of the system, not an evenly distributed one if you wish, but still the system under which this country as a whole has been making great progress in the last few years.
In that light it is not a resolution that we can accept because I do not think we should be called upon to accept blame. I do not think I should add anything because the hon. member would say that it is just another speech. He would be right, it would be another speech. I do hope that in the effort that is to be required from the Canadian people and from Canadian industry, there will be other manifestations than speeches to bring about the kind of situation which the hon. member would like to see prevailing in the region he so well represents in this house.

speechtext:
-in reply to what I think was a moderate presentation by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis). As for the resolution being a condemnation of the government, let me read what it says. It reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to a program for the decentralization of industry, so as to make possible a more balanced economy and for protection in the event of war.

Let me point out that in every one of the democratic countries decentralization is being considered as a defence measure. Discussions are going on at Washington in the United States as to how best industry can be decentralized. As far as I am aware the same kind of consideration is being given, to the decentralization of industry in the United Kingdom and elsewhere. That consideration has been given there for the past several years. As a matter of fact, vast new industries have been established -away from the eastern side of the United Kingdom in South Wales, Cumberland and other parts of the country where there were resources and unemployed people. Surely the suggestion that the government give consideration to the decentralization of industry should not be looked upon as a condemnation of the government unless the government is not prepared to take steps to assist in the decentralization of industry in this country.
Let me remind the Prime Minister and hon. gentlemen in this house that some of us come from parts of the country where our constituents have had to sell in an unprotected world market and buy in a highly protected market. Those who have bought supplies in the protected market of Canada have in large measure paid for the establishment of industry in the centralized provinces of Canada.
The Prime Minister mentioned the automobile industry, and one could mention the textile and other industries that have grown rich and powerful behind a tariff wall. In some instances they are subsidiaries of corporations which are controlled outside of this country. None the less they have been built up-by concessions granted by successive governments and by the maintenance of a very high tariff wall around this country. Until very recently we could see General Motors of Canada protected from General Motors of the United States, and the Ford Company of Canada protected from the Ford Company of the United States.
The consumers or purchasers of cars or machines manufactured by these protected industries in Canada were paying $200, $300, $400 and $500 or more for exactly the same type of machine as was manufactured by the parent company on the other side of the line.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DECENTRALIZATION TO ENSURE MORE BALANCED ECONOMY AND PROVIDE PROTECTION IN TIME OF WAR
speechtext: Supposedly Liberal policy.

subtopic: DECENTRALIZATION TO ENSURE MORE BALANCED ECONOMY AND PROVIDE PROTECTION IN TIME OF WAR
speechtext:
May I point out to the Prime Minister that as I understand it the tradition of the Liberal party in the past was a free trade tradition. If I had been aware that this debate was coming up tonight I could have produced figures to show that in spite
Decentralization of Industry of the free trade professions of the Liberal party, between 1921 and 1930 the Liberal party maintained a higher rate of tariff on some of the things I have mentioned than was maintained by what we always assumed was the high tariff Conservative party which they succeeded in 1921. These figures are on the record. I have used them in the house before and I would have used them tonight had I known what the Prime Minister was going to say.
Moreover, I cannot quite understand why the Prime Minister seemed to think that this was a resolution formulated on a doctrinaire socialist policy. It is nothing of the kind. There was no question of a discussion of socialism and free enterprise. Had that been one of the problems I think one would make a rather different speech from the speech of the hon. member for Cape Breton South. One could have made a very good case for the public development of our natural resources had he been inclined to do so. I am not going to do that.
Having had some experience during the last war, both as to the decentralization of industry and the concessions which the government gave to industries in order to build them up in central Canada, I think the hon. member for Cape Breton South and those of us who come from western Canada have a perfect right to suggest that if encouragement is going to be given today to industry to expand or to establish itself in Canada, then an attempt should be made to decentralize industry across Canada.
I was a member of the war expenditures committee and I remember that the present Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) was also a member of that committee. I remember that the late G. G. McGeer came before that committee, of which the Minister of Fisheries and I were both members, at one period during the war and urged that, instead of the government of Canada making great concessions to the Algoma Steel Corporation to build and expand blast furnaces in central Canada, because we were constructing ships on the Pacific coast and required steel plates there, some attempt should be made to establish a steel industry on Vancouver island where there were both coal and iron ore in close proximity.
I remember very well how the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew), Mr. G. G. McGeer and those of us who supported that point of view on the committee were told by the steel controller that that would not be done at all, that there were established steel industries in certain areas of Canada, and that as long as they were established there that was where the steel industry was going to go.

Decentralization of Industry Moreover, he told us that the steel industry had been overbuilt in central Canada and that no more post-war capacity was required. Today of course we find that a considerable amount of new capacity is required.
Of course it is perfectly true, as my hon. friend said, that Canada's natural resources are being exploited for the benefit of corporations that have their headquarters, their capital and their profits, when the time comes to declare profits, in another country. It is perfectly true that the returns we should be getting from our own resources are being drained away from this country. As a matter of fact we know that plans are being made-and my hon. friend was right in mentioning this to the house tonight-for the building of great steel plants along the Atlantic coast of the United States, so that in a little while we shall see the spectacle of iron ore from Labrador and Ungava being transported down the Labrador coast, or by rail to a point near the mouth of the St. Lawrence and thence past the coast of Nova Scotia where, as my hon. friend said, the steel industry of Canada has existed to such a great extent. Canadian mills will be by-passed and the ore will go to United States1 mills in Massachusetts and Maine or elsewhere.

speechtext: Just as it goes from Steep Rock to Cleveland.
