speechtext:
Yes, just as it goes from Steep Rock to Cleveland at the present time, deposits out of which millions of dollars have been made over the years by corporations whose headquarters were not in this country. The Prime Minister says that the federal government did not make the concessions, that it was for example the Quebec government that made the concession regarding Ungava, or the Newfoundland government that made the concession regarding Labrador iron ore deposits. That is perfectly true but it was this government and this house that gave access to those fields by granting a charter- was it two years ago-to build the Quebec, North Shore and Labrador Railway for a distance of some 300 miles, if my memory serves me correctly.
Therefore when my hon. friend says that the Quebec government alienated these resources let us not forget that it was this parliament, this house and this government which made possible the transportation of these valuable resources to the United States by granting a charter for a railway. I think that the hon. member for Cape Breton South attempted to perform a service tonight. He attempted to introduce a resolution with the hope, as he said, that other members would participate in the debate, that other maritime


members would speak, that members from the prairie provinces and British Columbia would speak and that all would express themselves in favour of the diffusion of industry throughout Canada as far as we are able to do so. Bear this in mind, that we can exercise a considerable amount of influence in the diffusion of industry.
My mind goes back to the last war. What did we do? We gave accelerated depreciation to corporations that were extending their plants or building new plants. What was that accelerated depreciation? We gave corporations the right to charge, in the prices that they charged the people of Canada, an amount sufficient to write off the capital outlay of the plant and machines within two years in some cases, and in a number of cases within four years. If the government grants accelerated depreciation what is actually being done is that we say to the corporation: You build the plant, the people of Canada will pay for it, and at the end of the time you will own it.
Not only that; in some instances we said to them: You can charge into your selling price an amount that will enable you to collect on your product a sufficient sum to retire the value of the plant you have built. With respect to some of these plants at least I have noticed that when we allowed them to charge so much more than was necessary to return a fair profit on their investment and to pay for their plants in wartime we set a price level which they have been maintaining ever since. I have not noticed a drop in the price level of some of these commodities produced in plants that were written off by accelerated depreciation and paid for by the Canadian people.
Therefore I say to the Prime Minister that my hon. friend's plea tonight was reasonable. It was not based on a discussion of any partisan policy or any doctrinaire viewpoint. The idea of diffusion was brought forward exactly as similar ideas are being brought forward in other countries, as a war measure. We need diffusion. Look at the way in which industry was concentrated in this country during the last war. You only had to go to the Niagara peninsula, to Welland, St. Catharines, Hamilton and so on, to realize how concentrated industry has become. If we are going to be in danger of bombing, such concentrated industry will make a very ready target for bombs which may reach this country in the event of war.
Let us hope of course that will never happen. Nevertheless it seems to me that when my hon. friend rose to speak tonight he did so for the purpose of putting before the house and the government a problem which I think the Prime Minister would have been well

advised to allow private members of the house to discuss pretty thoroughly before rising to summarize the debate. I am quite sure that the Prime Minister did not do so intentionally but I sincerely hope that his remarks tonight will not inhibit members of the house from rising to their feet and saying what they would have said anyway.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to endorse the motion introduced by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis). I think there was considerable logic in his argument. I was a bit surprised to see the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) enter the debate as soon as he did, and to hear him make some of the statements that he made because, quite frankly, in the past war the government of the day lost a great opportunity to decentralize industry to quite an extent in Canada. I have not the figures before me at the moment, but during those years I remember discussing the hundreds of millions of dollars the government were spending to assist industry to produce more. I forget the percentages also, but I do know that by far the greater proportion of that money went to the two central provinces. There I think the government missed a great opportunity to decentralize.
The Prime Minister spoke about tariffs and protection. The people in the prairie provinces have laboured for a long time under protection, and today under this government I think we have more protection, much of it disguised, than at any time since confederation. That is my opinion in spite of all the statements that may come from members of the government. The Prime Minister also said the government had never done anything toward centralizing industry. Well, only a few years ago we had a concrete example in the case of a government-owned institution, Trans-Canada Air Lines. The headquarters of this great corporation were moved from Winnipeg to Montreal.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: DECENTRALIZATION TO ENSURE MORE BALANCED ECONOMY AND PROVIDE PROTECTION IN TIME OF WAR
speechtext: A good move.

subtopic: DECENTRALIZATION TO ENSURE MORE BALANCED ECONOMY AND PROVIDE PROTECTION IN TIME OF WAR
speechtext:
That was done by the government, and it is a matter of opinion whether it was a good or bad move. The premier of Manitoba, the heads of the chamber of commerce, the mayor of Winnipeg and representatives of many organizations came to Ottawa to interview the government in an attempt to retain Trans-Canada Air Lines in Winnipeg. That was a move by this government which brought one of its own institutions to the central provinces, and I do not think that was good business. With all this fear of atomic bombing if we have a war, certainly it was not good business. Winnipeg is about halfway across this country, and
Decentralization of Industry surely it was the logical place for the headquarters of that company. Many of the officials owned their own homes there, and had to dispose of them and move their families to Montreal.
On another occasion I dealt with another industrial development, the flax processing plants built in Ontario during the war years. I pointed out at that time, as I have done since, that practically all the flaxseed required for that processing is grown in the three prairie provinces. There we were with an overburdened transportation system, a shortage of rolling stock and a shortage of manpower, moving great quantities of flaxseed from the prairie provinces to Ontario for processing, then turning around and taking a large proportion of the by-products back to the prairies for feed.
This is a complicated business; one thing leads to another. Nearly all the large farm implement companies are located in Ontario, though it is quite true that was their own decision. Yet sixty per cent of their production is sold in the three prairie provinces, and the farmers out there have to pay the added freight. That is another thing you can never get away from. The people in the prairie provinces buy everything plus freight, while their grain, livestock and everything else is sold less freight. That in itself is a great handicap and I think is unfair. We have the great concentration of population in these central provinces. Those people have to be fed. Eastern farmers find it difficult to grow enough feed grain, so the taxpayers of Canada have to subsidize the movement of feed grains from the prairie provinces to the east. The farmer out there who produces the grain pays his share of taxation also. That was a war move, but you see what it has developed into. We are still doing it today, eight years later, and in the meantime we have spent something over $140 million of the taxpayers' money to move this grain to where it can be fed by the farmers living closer to the industrial sections; and this in spite of the fact that in one of the later war years Alberta produced more hogs than any other province in Canada. We hear so much of sound economics and sound finance, yet this is the complicated set-up the government are working us into by this business of centralizing industry of all sorts. There is just no end to it, and every move of that kind is an added burden to the taxpayers.
Then the Prime Minister said they would do everything possible to decentralize industry. Well, I am afraid nothing much has been done yet. Of all the defence contracts let in the past nine months, over eighty per

Decentralization of Industry cent have gone to the two central provinces again. It does not look as though much of an effort was being made to decentralize industry. I venture to say that with a little assistance many of those contracts could have been filled in the maritimes, the prairie provinces and the west coast.

I would be glad if the hon. gentleman could give the correct figure. As I say, I was quoting a press dispatch, and I assume those people had authentic figures.
Then there is the matter of this accelerated depreciation, which was mentioned by the previous speaker. This is a matter that has been quite a bother to me for the past few years. I had thought it was just as important that if a farmer were short of funds to produce worthwhile foodstuffs for the war effort, he should be assisted just as certain other industries were. I have never been able to understand why a good farm operator, who had to invest large sums in equipment or plant expansion, should not be allowed the same kind of depreciation as these industries mentioned a short time ago by the hon. member


for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), who were allowed to write off their added costs in two, three or four years. That is not permitted under the act. That is another very unfair regulation of the Department of National Revenue, and there are many instances of that kind in which I believe the government should give far greater leadership if they really wanted an all-out effort. I cannot say an all-out war effort, because this is really an effort to prevent war. We are hoping it will succeed, but it may lead to war.
I do not want to take more time this evening, but I would like to plead with the government again to use their great power and influence to decentralize industry, because certainly that would be in the interests of all parts and all citizens of Canada.

subtopic: DECENTRALIZATION TO ENSURE MORE BALANCED ECONOMY AND PROVIDE PROTECTION IN TIME OF WAR
speechtext: By decentralization of industry does the hon. member mean the giving out of war contracts in better proportion to the various provinces or does he mean to decentralize the industry that is carried on in this country as usual outside of war?

subtopic: DECENTRALIZATION TO ENSURE MORE BALANCED ECONOMY AND PROVIDE PROTECTION IN TIME OF WAR
speechtext: I mean both, Mr. Speaker. I gave one concrete example. You will realize that the matter of the processing of flaxseed for oil is quite essential apart from war. There is always a much greater demand in wartime, but it is essential at any time. That is one concrete example I gave. I said I thought those plants should be in the area where the flaxseed itself is produced. It would be much more economical. I was referring both to the letting of contracts and the furnishing of financial assistance to develop and expand industries in logical areas.

subtopic: DECENTRALIZATION TO ENSURE MORE BALANCED ECONOMY AND PROVIDE PROTECTION IN TIME OF WAR
speechtext:
I should like
to say, first of all, Mr. Speaker, that I do not think that the intervention of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) was intended in any sense to limit or to cut off debate on this resolution. I think it arose rather out of the Prime Minister's recognition of the importance of the subject matter of this resolution and his desire to place before the house once again the attitude of the government on this highly important question.
I am tempted to deal at some length with the remarks made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) in introducing this resolution. I do not, however, wish to take up the time of the house in doing so; but I should like to make one or two remarks in general with respect to his approach to this problem. The hon. member for Cape Breton South said, at one point in his speech, that over the last few years arguments have come from his side of the house bringing to the government's attention the problem of decentralization of industry; and

he created the distinct impression that it was only from his side of the house that those arguments had come. The hon. member knows as well as do I and other hon. members of this house that that statement simply is not in accordance with the facts.
The hon. member also stated that he gained the impression that some people were getting tired of hearing maritime complaints. I have discussed the maritime point of view in this house on a number of occasions; and in my experience here I have heard many members putting forward the maritime point of view. I have also heard it discussed many times in private. But in my experience at least no one that I know of tires of hearing the maritime point of view being fairly and properly expressed at any time in this house or outside of it. However, a good many people-including, I think, the vast majority of maritimers-are exceedingly tired of hearing the maritime point of view put forward in an unfair, impractical and distorted manner, as we have heard it put forward here tonight by the hon. member for Cape Breton South.
Later on I shall deal with one or two points that the hon. gentleman raised. However, in view of the debate that has already taken place in this house during the last three or four weeks, it is perhaps not necessary for me to point out to you, Mr. Speaker, the number of occasions on which hon. members on all sides of this house and from all parties have placed before the house and the government consideration of the maritime point of view with respect to the decentralization of industry and with respect to the necessity for that point of view being given full consideration.
We have heard the Prime Minister this evening in a speech which I considered showed a great deal of spirit and a great deal of sincere belief in the future, in an industrial sense, of every part of this country, not just the central portions of it. It was a speech which I do not think was heated in the sense in which the leader of the C.C.F. group seemed to think it was heated; it was not heated in the sense of any irritation with the hon. member for Cape Breton South or anything of that kind, in my opinion; but was heated in his interest and belief in the future of this country.
We had in this house several days ago the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). He set out the policy of the government which I believe is one dictated by reason and, in its broad concept, by the fundamental interests of this country. The Minister of Trade and Commerce pointed out to the house that, as to defence purchases
Decentralization of Industry or production, for defence, the government were ready and anxious to use every single facility that exists in this country, whether it is located in the east, in the west or in the central provinces. Their sole interest is to get production and to get produced the things that are needed. In reply to specific questions I think he indicated to hon. members that if they knew of any facilities which were available and which were not being used, all they had to do was to bring them to the attention of his department and every effort would be made to employ those facilities.
Then there is the question of the creation of new facilities. The Minister of Trade and Commerce stated the policy of the government by saying that there was nothing that received more immediate or more careful attention that the possibility of facilitating the creation of an industry in the maritime provinces, unless it was a similar possibility of establishing a new industry in the prairie provinces. So far as the government is able to influence matters of this kind, I am satisfied that that is a sincere statement of policy that will be carried out.
In discussing this matter, Mr. Speaker, I do not think that we should lose sight of the fact that in many ways and to a large extent this question of the decentralization of industry and the wider expansion of new industry is a matter of self-help. It is going to be largely a matter of co-operative effort between private industry in the various parts of this country, provincial governments and the federal government. The expansion of industry, which is of the greatest value to the parts of this country that have not reached the stage of industrialization enjoyed by the central provinces, is that of private industry which is intended to serve not simply defence needs but the ordinary needs of the consumers of this country.
As hon. members know, the establishment of these industries depends very largely on the question of facilities, the availability of labour, materials and any advantages that location may give. I feel that, so far as the maritimes are concerned, in the past we have fallen down in emphasizing and making use of the location and other advantages that we enjoy. It is the fault of many individuals, of the attitude of many people in various industries, and that sort of thing, in the maritime provinces. But that is a difficulty which I believe is being overcome.
In the maritime provinces there is a new spirit of initiative in industry generally that is having a very good effect, and which will have a much broader effect in the days to come.

Decentralization of Industry
One of the considerations of overriding importance which we are going to have to face in the maritime provinces is the question of the provision of sources of power for new industry, if we are interested in seeing new industry established in those provinces. One of the great factors that made industrial development so concentrated in the central part of this country was the provision of adequate power facilities, and if we are to compete we must have those facilities ourselves.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) spoke of the number of small industries which existed in Nova Scotia in the days of confederation which have since disappeared. I am sure we all regret the passing of small industries of that kind, but I submit to him and to the house that his argument that the disappearance of these small industries was the result of confederation and the centralizing influences that took place after that time is hardly correct. The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that at the time of confederation it was a day of small industries. There were small industries of the type he mentions all over Ontario and Quebec and in the states of the United States; but with the development of better communication facilities and things of that sort, and the development of the economy, these small industries gradually became absorbed into larger industries. A similar argument could be made for various locations in other parts of the country which could not possibly be considered to be a result of confederation.
I should like to point out to him that these developments which took place were not all bad. The same forces that caused the smaller industries to be absorbed were the only forces that made it possible for the great development of the coal and steel industry in his own part of the island of Cape Breton. Without these additional or new means of communication, the railway and that sort of thing, that great industrial development would not have been possible. We might still have had a cotton mill at Yarmouth, or wherever it was, that he was referring to, but we would not have the great industrial development of his own area.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Cape Breton South ended his argument by repeating something he had said on two occasions in his speech, namely, that nothing had been done. I submit that is the kind of argument that is objectionable, and which does not add anything to advance the cause that he has in mind in putting this resolution before the house. The fact is that a great deal has been accomplished. It is not exactly my idea of the best way of


improving a situation to submit that improvements which have taken place do not exist at all.
The other day the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) mentioned in the house, and I have also mentioned in the house, the development of the Fairey Aviation Company (Canada) Limited at Eastern Passage in Halifax. That is very largely a defence industry, but it is located where it is only because of the kind of co-operative effort that I have referred to earlier, namely, the desire of this government to see any industry which could possibly be located in the east located there, the desire of the provincial government to see a new industry located in the province, and the desire of an industrial organization to seize certain real advantages which they saw in the situation, and which they found in that part of the country. Through that co-operative effort, and through taking advantage of those circumstances, we have a thriving and useful industry. I would also use the example of the plant of Cossor (Canada) Limited which has been established in Halifax, through the operation of the same circumstances, and which is developing very nicely. Therefore I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Cape Breton South does not do his cause any good, and he does not do the interests of the maritime provinces any good, by pretending that these accomplishments just do not exist.
The resolution reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to a program for the decentralization of industry-
And so on. This wording carries with it, I believe, the very kind of argumentation to which I objected in the speech of the mover of the resolution. It is clearly intended to create the impression: (1), that the government has not any program or policy, which is contrary to the statements of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent); and (2), that nothing has been done along this line. I am unable to agree with this line of argument, Mr. Speaker, and I think that it would not serve the interests of industrial development in the maritime provinces or anywhere else in Canada for this house to pass a resolution which so clearly and intentionally carries these implications.

Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey) has said, this subject has been debated in the house on many occasions. As a matter of fact I have spoken on a number of occasions about the decentralization of industry.

I am sorry I was not in the house when the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) spoke, but I have been assured that he put up a very able argument, as we would expect from him. Judging from the criticism which has come from the other side of the house, I am convinced that it must have been a most able presentation.
As the hon. member for Halifax has said, this matter has been discussed on many occasions; but as Mark Twain once said about the weather, it is talked and talked about, but there is never anything done about it. That is really what we in the maritime provinces are objecting to.
This evening I listened to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) give us something of the history of the Hudson's Bay Company, and some other history of Canada. Well, history is very interesting indeed. I would point out that it was in the maritime provinces that history was first made in Canada. Unfortunately however it was in the early days, and today the people of the maritime provinces feel they cannot live on the history of the past. For instance, at the time of confederation the city of Saint John built more ships than any other port of the North American continent. It was at that time the fourth greatest shipping port of the world. In 1867 Saint John had a population of almost forty thousand, and today her population is not much greater. This fact alone speaks volumes about what has happened to the maritime provinces.
It is not my intention to go into detail, because those details have been mentioned many times. The fact remains however that those of us in the maritime provinces, and particularly in New Brunswick, are not receiving our full share of attention from this government, and have not from governments in the past.
The Prime Minister referred to bank presidents. I could tell him that not only bank presidents but also the heads of manufacturing concerns, educational leaders, ministers and the like have come from the maritimes and made their mark in other parts of Canada. We export the brains to run the business in Ontario and Quebec.
We would like to keep those people in our own part of the country. We want to have business down there, so that those people could look after our banks, our manufacturing, our industries and our educational institutions. A few days ago when discussing education I said that the maritime provinces are held up as a horrible example, so far as education is concerned. The reason is, of
Decentralization of Industry
course, that we have not the money with which to pay for education.
All that the people in our provinces are asking today is that they be given equal opportunity with the rest of Canada, so that they may educate their children, keep their young men at home, and be placed in the same position as other parts of Canada. That is all we are asking.
I was interested to hear what the leader of the C.C.F. had to say. He spoke about the depressed areas of Great Britain. I remember that in 1944 I happened to be in England, in company with Mr. Bracken. While there we met some of the members of Mr. Churchill's cabinet, and spoke particularly with Mr. Hugh Dalton who told us that at that time they were looking after the depressed areas in Great Britain. He said for instance that the people up in the Durham area and the people in Wales were not in as prosperous condition as those in other parts of the country, but that the government was going to move industry to those parts of Great Britain so that people in all parts of the country would enjoy the same privileges.
That is exactly what the people of the maritimes are now asking the government of Canada to do-and I believe it can be done. The hon. member for Halifax raised some of the objections as to why he feels we cannot have an equal share of industry. In this connection he mentioned the development of electrical power. It is true that the electrical power has not been developed to the same extent in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island as it has been in other parts of Canada. I believe we have the facilities and opportunities there for the development of power. Given some assistance, I believe we could develop it and, with that electrical power, we could manufacture just as cheaply down there as it can be done in any other part of the country.
We have the raw material and we have the manpower. There is more idle manpower in the maritime provinces than in any other part of Canada. Today manpower is one of the greatest essentials, so far as manufacturing in this country is concerned. A few days age I was told of a New Brunswicker who opened a factory just outside Toronto to fill shells. He sent a team down to New Brunswick to round up men who would come back to Toronto to work in his factory. It does not require much electrical power to fill shells. That work could have been done in the maritime provinces, down near the city of Saint John, just as well as it can be done near Toronto. Further than that, if those shells are being prepared for use in Europe, to assist our
706

Decentralization of Industry allies over there in the event of war, then they must be shipped to Saint John or to Halifax to be sent overseas.
These are the things to which we object, Mr. Speaker. Then, a word about housing. I could show hon. members many vacant houses in our towns and villages in my own province. Those houses are deserted because the people are leaving. I am sure the minister will agree that housing in the maritime provinces is not as great a problem as it is around Toronto, Montreal or Hamilton, Why, then, should we take men away from their homes in the maritimes and bring them to Ontario and Quebec to do work, when that work could be done down by the sea, and the people would have decent houses in which to live.
The people of the maritimes are basing their fears of what may happen now on what happened during the last war. We were not given our just rights; there can be no question about that. Anyone who has read the Saint John Telegraph-Journal for the last two weeks will know that there have been editorials on the front page of that newspaper setting out the situation in that part of the world. They give a break-down of second war contracts for the different provinces to show the great injustice and the great inequalities there were during that war.
These figures show that in Prince Edward Island, with a population, according to the 1941 census, of 95,047, the amount spent per head on war contracts was $73.65; in Nova Scotia, with a population of 577,962, the amount spent per head was $509.55. They did fairly well. But in New Brunswick, with a population of 457,401, we received $172.70 per head.
Then, coming to Quebec, with a population of 3,331,882, the amount spent per head was $1,576.75 and in Ontario, with a population of 3,787,655, the amount spent per head was $1,435.35. 1 shall not give the figures for the other provinces. Those will be sufficient to show the picture during the last war. That is why the people in the maritime provinces today, realizing that there is not a state of war at this time, and realizing that possibly during the last war the government had to develop industry where the factories were located, are taking a keen interest in the matter. There is no great war on at the present time and it would be possible for the government to make a thorough survey of the maritime provinces and Canada generally, and that is all this resolution asks for. If they do that and if they have any intention to do justice to our part of the country they will find that we can manufacture two, three,


yes I would say even four times as much as we are at the present time. During the last war with four per cent of the population of Canada we had less than one-half of one per cent of the production.
I do not think it is necessary for me to press this point any further as it is quite clear. If the government is anxious to assist the people in these provinces, to keep them from moving to other parts of Canada, to provide them with money with which to carry on schools, churches and other services, they will pay more attention to them. They should act as they have acted in Great Britain where certain areas were treated as being more or less depressed.
Most hon. members from the maritime provinces sit on the other side of the house. There are only a few of us on this side, like the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black) and the hon. member for Queens and myself. I should like to hear the voices of all hon. members from the maritime provinces raised in this house as well as in their caucus so that something will be done to help this part of Canada.

speechtext:
I hear some hon. members saying "Wrong page". There are so many examples of the extent to which this government has within its hands to control the destiny of Canada, without any measure of actual supervision by parliament, that it is just about time for the members of this house to decide whether in fact we have a dictatorship or responsible government. If some hon. members would listen to the parliamentary principles which have been expounded in this house by one of their own number, the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), who I hope will be repeating some of those basic principles elsewhere in this city this evening or some other time during the next day or two, they might begin to assert some of those basic truths which were supposed to be part and parcel of the name Liberal. As it stands at the moment the only thing that seems to be Liberal about this party is its liberal expenditure of public money without affording parliament any opportunity to decide how that money is going to be spent.
The suggestion of innocent lack of authority over industry would almost seem to indicate that the government thinks memories are very short. Some people here will remember the annoyance expressed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) in different ways when some time was spent

Decentralization of Industry last year in determining where certain pipe lines were to go. That was a matter under the authority of this government; and those pipe lines will have a great deal to do with where certain industries will be located. Some hon, members will recall that one of the iron developments mentioned here this evening, Steep Rock, has had a great deal of assistance from the government. I am not questioning the value of that development, but most certainly this government had something to do with how that ore was to be shipped) and delivered. This government has evolved a system which places a very real restraint upon the freedom of risk capital in deciding exactly where some of it will go. I do not suggest for one moment that many will not determine and insist upon determining where they shall go; but others, from the very nature of the enterprise in which they are going to engage, most certainly will be guided by the gentle suggestion of the Minister of Trade and Commerce as to what would be most acceptable to the government.
Then other hon. members will recall that in the last world war very large sums of money were spent by this government on the construction of one of the largest electrical power-producing plants in Canada. I am not entering into any debate now as to the merits or otherwise of the ultimate disposition of that plant, but certainly the government has a good deal of influence over where some of these developments take place. And I would point out that electrical energy is available for development in many parts of this country, including the maritime provinces. This is particularly true of our newest province, Newfoundland. There are immense undeveloped water resources in that province which, if developed under plans similar to those put into effect elsewhere in Canada, could be used by great industries at tidewater, using raw materials coming by ship from other parts of the world and shipping the finished products to the places in Canada and
outside where they might be required. In the maritime provinces, in addition to water resources available for development, there are also coal resources from which electricity can be produced in very large quantities.
I am not in any way confining my thoughts to the maritime provinces. Right across Canada there are great opportunities for using our power resources to open up new industry and distribute the concentration of population in exactly the way that has been urged by those engaged in civil defence activities. Either there needs to be some reconciliation between the point of view of the government and the agencies dealing with civil defence, or this resolution should be acceptable to the government because it is the very thing civil defence agencies have been urging. I do suggest that this resolution, far from condemning the government, simply states a proposition which every hon. member of this house could well support, with the idea of spreading the population of this country, decentralizing concentration of population, employing those who are now living in areas where employment is not to be found in the way that it should be, and generally strengthening the whole economy of Canada.
On motion of Mr. McLure the debate was adjourned.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Tomorrow being government day we shall proceed with the resolution to introduce a bill to amend the Indian Act; then we shall consider Bill No. 24, to confer certain emergency powers upon the governor in council. Having disposed of those two items we shall take up, but I cannot indicate in what order, Bill No. 5, Bill No. 6 and Bill No. 76.
It being five minutes after eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
